nodes.name: Riesz-Kantorovich Theorem
nodes.statement: If $L$ is an ordered vector space with the Riesz Decomposition Property and $M$ is a Dedekind complete vector lattice, then the ordered vector space $\blinop {L} {M}$ of order bounded linear operators between $L$ and $M$ is a Dedekind complete vector lattice. Moreover, if $S, T \in \blinop {L} {M}$, then for each $x \in L_+$ we have \begin{gather} [S \vee T] (x) = \sup \{S y + T (x - y) \mid 0 \leqslant y \leqslant x \}, \\ [S \wedge T] (x) = \inf \{S y + T (x - y) \mid 0 \leqslant y \leqslant x \}. \end{gather}
nodes.origin_citation: M. Riesz 1940; L. V. Kantorovich 1936 (as quoted from Aliprantis & Tourky 2002)
assumptions: $L$ is an ordered vector space with the Riesz Decomposition Property
$M$ is a Dedekind complete vector lattice
$S, T \in \blinop {L} {M}$
$x \in L_+$
conclusions: the ordered vector space $\blinop {L} {M}$ of order bounded linear operators between $L$ and $M$ is a Dedekind complete vector lattice
[S \vee T] (x) = \sup \{S y + T (x - y) \mid 0 \leqslant y \leqslant x \},
[S \wedge T] (x) = \inf \{S y + T (x - y) \mid 0 \leqslant y \leqslant x \}.
the ordered vector space $\blinop {L} {M}$ of order bounded linear operators between $L$ and $M$ is a Dedekind complete vector lattice

$x \in L_+$

nodes.statement_short: With RDP domain and Dedekind complete codomain, order bounded operators form a Dedekind complete lattice with sup/inf given by the RK formulae.

nodes.name: Order bounded operators are regular under Riesz-Kantorovich conditions
nodes.statement: In particular, this theorem implies that under its conditions every order bounded operator $T : L \to M$ is regular.

nodes.name: Riesz-Kantorovich formulae
nodes.statement:
Equations \eqref {stvee} and \eqref {stwedge} and their variants describing the lattice operations of $\blinop {L} {M}$
are known as the \emph {Riesz-Kantorovich formulae}.

nodes.name: Riesz-Kantorovich formula problem
nodes.statement:
Related to these formulae is the following long-standing problem
that was posed in a number of slightly different versions (see, e.~g., \cite [\S 2] {positiveoperators}, \cite {aliprantistourky2002}):
if a supremum of two linear opeartors $S, T \in \mathcal L$ exists in a linear space $\mathcal L$ of linear operators between $L$ and $M$
(where of special interest are the space of order bounded operators and the space of regular operators), is it given by a Riesz-Kantorovich formula?
nodes.origin_citation: Aliprantis & Burkinshaw, Positive Operators; Aliprantis & Tourky 2002
also_stated_at:
As it was explained in Section~\ref {ovl},
there is a long-standing open problem that can be rephrased as follows:
is it possible to characterize linearity of the Riesz-Kantorovich transform of a particular
finite collection $T$ of linear operators in terms of the existence of the supremum of $T$ in an ordered space of linear operators?
nodes.statement_short: Does a supremum of two operators in a space of linear operators, when it exists, coincide with the Riesz-Kantorovich formula?

nodes.name: Ordered linear space
nodes.statement:
An \emph {ordered linear space} $X$, also called an \emph {ordered vector space}, is a linear space
(we only consider spaces over the field of reals $\mathbb R$) equipped with a partial order
$\geqslant$ which is consistent with the linear structure, that is for all $x, y, z \in V$ such that $x \geqslant y$
and $\lambda \geqslant 0$ we have $x + z \geqslant y + z$ and $\lambda x \geqslant \lambda y$.
differentia: equipped with a partial order $\geqslant$ which is consistent with the linear structure
nodes.statement_short: A real linear space with a partial order compatible with addition and nonnegative scaling.

nodes.name: Nonnegative cone
nodes.statement:
The order $\geqslant$ is completely determined by the \emph {nonnegative cone} $X_+ = \{x \in X \mid x \geqslant 0\}$
(which is a convex pointed cone) in the sense that every convex cone $K \subset X$ of a linear space $X$ such that $K \cap (-K) = \{0\}$
determines a unique order ($x \geqslant y$ if and only if $x - y \in K$) that turns $X$ into an ordered linear space satisfying $X_+ = K$.
nodes.statement_short: The order is determined by its nonnegative cone $X_+$, and every pointed convex cone defines an order.

nodes.name: Generating cone
nodes.statement:
We say that a cone $X_+$ is \emph {generating in $X$} if $X = X_+ - X_+$, that is for any $x \in X$ there exist some
$y, z \in X_+$ such that $x = y - z$.

nodes.name: Order interval
nodes.statement:
Let $X$ be an ordered linear space.
An \emph {order interval} between a couple of points $x, y \in X$ such that $y \geqslant x$ is the set
$[x, y] = \{ z \in X \mid x \leqslant z \leqslant y \}$.

nodes.name: Order bounded set
nodes.statement:
We say that a set $A \subset X$ is \emph {order bounded} if
$A \subset [x, y]$ for some $x, y \in X$, $y \geqslant x$.

nodes.name: Upper bound
nodes.statement:
If $y \geqslant x$ for all $x \in A$ then $y$ is called an \emph {upper bound} of $A$;
we sometimes denote it by $y \geqslant A$.

nodes.name: Supremum
nodes.statement:
If there exists some $x \in X$ such that $y \geqslant x$ for any upper bound $y$ of $A$, i.~e. if $x$ is the \emph {least upper bound} of $A$,
then $x$ is called the \emph {supremum} of $A$ and we denote this
fact by $x = \sup A$.

nodes.name: Infimum
nodes.statement: Likewise, $x$ is called an \emph {infinum} of $A$, $x = \inf A$, if $x$ is the greatest lower bound.

nodes.name: Space of linear operators
nodes.statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be linear spaces.  We denote by $\linop {X} {Y}$ the set of all linear operators $T : X \to Y$.

nodes.name: Space of continuous linear operators
nodes.statement:
If, additionally,
$X$ and $Y$ are equipped with topologies turning them into topological linear spaces,
we denote by $\clinop {X} {Y} \subset \linop {X} {Y}$ the set of all continuous operators.

nodes.name: Order bounded map
nodes.statement:
Now suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces.
We say that a (not necessarily linear) map
$T : X \to Y$ is \emph {order bounded} if its values $T (A) = \{ T x \mid x \in A \}$ on order bounded sets $A \subset X$ are
order bounded.
differentia: its values $T (A) = \{ T x \mid x \in A \}$ on order bounded sets $A \subset X$ are order bounded

nodes.name: Positive map
nodes.statement: $T$ is called \emph {positive} if $T x \geqslant 0$ for all $x \in X_+$; we denote this fact by $T \geqslant 0$.

nodes.name: Strictly positive map
nodes.statement: $T$ is called \emph {strictly positive} if $T x > 0$ for all $x \in X_+ \setminus \{0\}$.

nodes.name: Order on maps
nodes.statement:
We say that $S \geqslant T$ for some $S : X \to Y$ if $S - T \geqslant 0$; this defines a natural partial order
on the set of all maps $T : X \to Y$.

nodes.name: Regular operator
nodes.statement:
$T$ is called \emph {regular} if $T \in \linop {X} {Y}$ and
$T = U - V$ for some positive $U, V \in \linop {X} {Y}$.
differentia: $T = U - V$ for some positive $U, V \in \linop {X} {Y}$

nodes.name: Spaces of order bounded and regular operators
nodes.statement:
We denote the set of order bounded linear operators between ordered linear spaces $X$ and $Y$ by $\blinop {X} {Y}$,
and likewise the set of regular operators between $X$ and $Y$ by $\rlinop {X} {Y}$.

nodes.name: Positive operators are order bounded
nodes.statement:
It is easy to see that every positive linear operator is order bounded
and thus $\rlinop {X} {Y} \subset \blinop {X} {Y}$; this inclusion may be proper in general.
conclusions: every positive linear operator is order bounded
$\rlinop {X} {Y} \subset \blinop {X} {Y}$

nodes.name: Lexicographic plane
nodes.statement:
Both of these sets of operators may be very narrow: for example, if $X = \mathbb R^2$ is the plane with the lexicographic
order $X_+ = \left\{ (x, y) \mid \text {either $y > 0$ or $y = 0$ and $x \geqslant 0$} \right\}$
then $\rlinop {X} {\mathbb R} = \blinop {X} {\mathbb R} = \{f \mid f (x, y) = \alpha y \}$, and in general
ordered linear spaces with the lexicographic order have one-dimensional duals $\rlinop {X} {\mathbb R} = \blinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ irrespective to
the (finite or infinite) dimension of $X$.
nodes.statement_short: With lexicographic order on $\mathbb R^2$ the order bounded and regular duals are one-dimensional.

nodes.name: Superadditive and additive maps
Superlinear and linear maps on a cone
nodes.statement:
If, in addition, $T$ is \emph {positively homogeneous},
that is $T (\lambda x) = \lambda T (x)$ for all $\lambda \geqslant 0$ and $x \in X_+$, we say that $T$ is
\emph {superlinear} and \emph {linear} respectively.

nodes.name: Unique linear extension from a generating cone
nodes.statement:
If the cone $X_+$ is generating in $X$ then any linear map $T : X_+ \to Y$
can be uniquely extended to a linear map on all $X$ by setting $T x = T y - T z$ for $x = y - z$, $x \in X$, $y, z \in X_+$.
assumptions: the cone $X_+$ is generating in $X$
conclusions: any linear map $T : X_+ \to Y$ can be uniquely extended to a linear map on all $X$

nodes.name: Set of superlinear maps
nodes.statement: We denote the set of all superlinear maps $T : X_+ \to Y$ by \suplinop {X_+} {Y}.

nodes.name: Riesz Decomposition Property
Riesz Decomposition Property equals interpolation property
nodes.statement:
It is well known that the Riesz Decomposition Property is equivalent to the \emph {interpolation property}: for any finite $A, B \subset X$ such that
$A \leqslant B$ in the sense that $a \leqslant b$ for all $a \in A$ and $b \in B$ there exists some $x \in X$ such that
$A \leqslant x \leqslant B$, i.~e. $a \leqslant x \leqslant b$ for all $a \in A$ and $b \in B$.
conclusions: the Riesz Decomposition Property is equivalent to the \emph {interpolation property}
equivalent_conditions: for any finite $A, B \subset X$ such that $A \leqslant B$ in the sense that $a \leqslant b$ for all $a \in A$ and $b \in B$ there exists some $x \in X$ such that $A \leqslant x \leqslant B$
nodes.statement_short: RDP is equivalent to the interpolation property for finite sets; this also defines the interpolation property.

nodes.name: Lattice (Riesz space)
nodes.statement:
An ordered linear space $X$ is said to be a \emph {lattice} or \emph {Riesz space} if for any $x, y \in X$ the supremum $x \vee y = \sup \{x, y\}$
exists in $X$.
differentia: for any $x, y \in X$ the supremum $x \vee y = \sup \{x, y\}$ exists in $X$

nodes.name: Infima, positive parts and moduli
nodes.statement:
If this is the case then infinums $x \wedge y = -[(-x) \vee (-y)]$, positive parts $x^+ = x \vee 0$
and moduli $|x| = x \vee (-x)$ also exist.

nodes.name: Lattices have the Riesz Decomposition Property
nodes.statement: A lattice always has the Riesz Decomposition Property.
conclusions: A lattice always has the Riesz Decomposition Property.

nodes.name: Dedekind complete space
nodes.statement:
An ordered linear space $X$ is called \emph {Dedekind complete} (or just \emph {complete}) if any set $A \subset X$ that has an upper bound also
has a supremum 
$\sup A$.
differentia: any set $A \subset X$ that has an upper bound also has a supremum

nodes.name: Hahn-Banach Theorem
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces, $Y$ is Dedekind complete, $L \subset X$ is a linear space such that $X_+ + L = X$, $p : X_+ \to Y$ is a superlinear map and $T_0 : L \to Y$ is a linear operator satisfying $T_0 x \geqslant p (x)$ for all $x \in L \cap X_+$. Then there exists an extension $T \in \linop {X} {Y}$ of $T_0$ satisfying $T x \geqslant p (x)$ for all $x \in X_+$.
assumptions: $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces
$Y$ is Dedekind complete
$L \subset X$ is a linear space such that $X_+ + L = X$
$p : X_+ \to Y$ is a superlinear map
$T_0 : L \to Y$ is a linear operator satisfying $T_0 x \geqslant p (x)$ for all $x \in L \cap X_+$
conclusions: there exists an extension $T \in \linop {X} {Y}$ of $T_0$ satisfying $T x \geqslant p (x)$ for all $x \in X_+$
nodes.statement_short: Hahn-Banach extension with a superlinear minorant on the cone into a Dedekind complete space.

nodes.name: Sublinear formulation of Hahn-Banach
nodes.statement:
This theorem is nearly always formulated with sublinear majorants $q = -p$, but superlinear minorants
suit the purposes of the present work better.

nodes.name: Hahn-Banach-Kantorovich and M. Riesz extension theorems as special cases
nodes.statement:
Setting $X_+ = X$ (i.~e. considering the full order, that is $x \geqslant y$ for all $x, y \in X$;
the assumption that $X_+$ is a partial order is not actually used)
yields what is often called the
Hahn-Banach-Kantorovich theorem (\cite {kantorovich1935}); letting $p = 0$ produces the
M.~Riesz extension theorem (\cite {riesz1923}).
nodes.statement_short: With $X_+ = X$ one gets the Hahn-Banach-Kantorovich theorem; with $p = 0$ the M. Riesz extension theorem.

nodes.name: Proof sketch of the Hahn-Banach Theorem
nodes.statement:
Let us give a sketch of the proof. 
By the standard inductive reasoning it is sufficient to consider the case
$\dim X \slash L = 1$.  We fix some $x_0 \in X \setminus L$;
then $X = \{x + s x_0 \mid x \in L, s \in \mathbb R\}$ and
we need to define a value $y_0 \in Y$ in such a way that an extension
$T (x + s x_0) = T_0 x + s y_0$ would satisfy the necessary estimate
$T (x + s x_0) \geqslant p (x + s x_0)$ whenever $x + s x_0 \in X_+$.
Considering different signs of $s$ we see that this is equivalent to
\begin{equation} T_0 u - p (u - x_0) \geqslant y_0 \geqslant p (v + x_0) - T_0 v
\end{equation}
for all $u, v \in L$ satisfying $u - x_0 \in X_+$ and $v + x_0 \in X_+$.
Observe that such $u$ and $v$ always exist since
by the assumptions
$$
X_+ + L = X = -X = -(X_+ + L) = -X_+ - L = -X_+ + L,
$$
and for any such $u$ and $v$ we have $u + v = (u - x_0) + (v + x_0) \in X_+ \cap L$, so
$$
T_0 u + T_0 v = T_0 (u + v) \geqslant p (u + v) = p ([u - x_0] + [v + x_0]) \geqslant p (u - x_0) + p (v + x_0)
$$
by superlinearity of $p$, which implies that
\begin{equation} T_0 u - p (u - x_0) \geqslant p (v + x_0) - T_0 v
\end{equation}
for any $u, v \in L$ satisfying $u - x_0 \in X_+$ and $v + x_0 \in X_+$.
From \eqref {hbk1} it is clear that the set of values of the right-hand part of~\eqref {hbk}
has an upper bound, and the least upper bound of the right-hand part is also a lower bound for the left-hand part.
Thus we may set
$$
y_0 = \sup \{p (v + x_0) - T_0 v \mid v + x_0 \in X_+\}
$$
and conclude that $y_0$ satisfies the required estimates~\eqref {hbk}.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce by induction to codimension one, then choose the value at $x_0$ as a supremum squeezed between two bounds given by superlinearity.

nodes.name: Reduction to codimension one
nodes.statement:
Let us give a sketch of the proof. 
By the standard inductive reasoning it is sufficient to consider the case
$\dim X \slash L = 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to codimension one by induction

nodes.name: Extension ansatz
nodes.statement:
We fix some $x_0 \in X \setminus L$;
then $X = \{x + s x_0 \mid x \in L, s \in \mathbb R\}$ and
we need to define a value $y_0 \in Y$ in such a way that an extension
$T (x + s x_0) = T_0 x + s y_0$ would satisfy the necessary estimate

nodes.name: Two-sided bound on y_0
nodes.statement:
Considering different signs of $s$ we see that this is equivalent to
\begin{equation} T_0 u - p (u - x_0) \geqslant y_0 \geqslant p (v + x_0) - T_0 v
\end{equation}
for all $u, v \in L$ satisfying $u - x_0 \in X_+$ and $v + x_0 \in X_+$.
nodes.statement_short: Reformulate the requirement as the two-sided bound (hbk) on $y_0$

nodes.name: Compatibility of bounds
nodes.statement:
Observe that such $u$ and $v$ always exist since
by the assumptions
$$
X_+ + L = X = -X = -(X_+ + L) = -X_+ - L = -X_+ + L,
$$
and for any such $u$ and $v$ we have $u + v = (u - x_0) + (v + x_0) \in X_+ \cap L$, so
$$
T_0 u + T_0 v = T_0 (u + v) \geqslant p (u + v) = p ([u - x_0] + [v + x_0]) \geqslant p (u - x_0) + p (v + x_0)
$$
by superlinearity of $p$, which implies that
\begin{equation} T_0 u - p (u - x_0) \geqslant p (v + x_0) - T_0 v
\end{equation}
for any $u, v \in L$ satisfying $u - x_0 \in X_+$ and $v + x_0 \in X_+$.
nodes.statement_short: Superlinearity of $p$ shows the lower bounds never exceed the upper bounds

nodes.name: Supremum lies between bounds
nodes.statement:
From \eqref {hbk1} it is clear that the set of values of the right-hand part of~\eqref {hbk}
has an upper bound, and the least upper bound of the right-hand part is also a lower bound for the left-hand part.
nodes.statement_short: The right-hand sides are bounded above and their sup is below the left-hand sides

Thus we may set
$$
y_0 = \sup \{p (v + x_0) - T_0 v \mid v + x_0 \in X_+\}
$$
and conclude that $y_0$ satisfies the required estimates~\eqref {hbk}.

nodes.name: Internal point
nodes.statement:
Let $X$ be a linear space.
We say that $e \in A$ is an \emph {internal point} of a set $A \subset X$
(sometimes also called a \emph {core point} or an \emph {algebraically interior point})
if for any $x \in A$ there exists some $\varepsilon > 0$ such that $e + \alpha x \in A$ for all values $\alpha \in \mathbb R$
satisfying $-\varepsilon < \alpha < \varepsilon$.
differentia: for any $x \in A$ there exists some $\varepsilon > 0$ such that $e + \alpha x \in A$ for all values $\alpha \in \mathbb R$ satisfying $-\varepsilon < \alpha < \varepsilon$

nodes.name: Set of internal points
nodes.statement: We denote the set of internal points of $A$ by $\mathrm{int} A$.

nodes.name: Line-open set
nodes.statement:
With only a limited number of caveats the \emph {line-open sets} $A$,
i.~e. the sets $A \subset X$ such that $A = \mathrm{int} A$, behave very much like open sets in a Hausdorff linear topological
space.

nodes.name: Convex combination with an internal point is internal
nodes.statement:
A convex combination $(1 - \theta) y + \theta x$, $0 < \theta < 1$, of an internal point $x \in \mathrm{int} A$ of $A$ and some $y \in A$ is also an internal point
of $A$.
assumptions: $0 < \theta < 1$
$x \in \mathrm{int} A$
$y \in A$
conclusions: is also an internal point of $A$

nodes.name: Order unit
nodes.statement:
Now let $X$ be an ordered linear space.
A vector $e \in X_+$ is called an \emph {order unit} of $X$ if for any $x \in X$ there exists
some $\lambda > 0$ such that $x \leqslant \lambda e$.

nodes.name: Order units are the internal points of the cone
nodes.statement:
It is well known that $e$ is an order unit of $X$ if and only if $e$ is an internal point of
$X_+$.
conclusions: $e$ is an order unit of $X$ if and only if $e$ is an internal point of $X_+$

nodes.name: Order topology
nodes.statement:
Let $X$ be an ordered linear space.
The \emph {order topology} of $X$ is the finest locally convex topology
that has a base of convex circled open neighbourhoods at $0$ that absorb every order interval of $X$;
this topology is Hausdorff if and only if $\blinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ separates points of $X$
(i.~e. if and only if $f (x) = 0$ for all $f \in \blinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ implies $x = 0$).
differentia: has a base of convex circled open neighbourhoods at $0$ that absorb every order interval of $X$
nodes.statement_short: The finest locally convex topology whose zero-neighbourhoods absorb order intervals; Hausdorff iff order bounded functionals separate points.

nodes.name: Order bounded functionals are continuous in the order topology
nodes.statement:
An important property of the order topology is that
$\blinop {X} {\mathbb R} = \clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ (see, e.~g., \cite [Theorem~2.69] {conesandduality}).
nodes.origin_citation: Aliprantis & Tourky, Cones and Duality (2007), Theorem 2.69
conclusions: $\blinop {X} {\mathbb R} = \clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$

nodes.name: Separation by a linear map
nodes.statement:
Suppose that $X$ is a linear space, $Y$ is an ordered linear space, $A \subset X$ is a convex set, $x \in X$ and $f \in \linop {X} {Y}$.
We say that \emph {$f$ separates $x$ from $A$} if either $f (x) \leqslant f (A)$ or $f (x) \geqslant f (A)$, where $f (A) = \{f (y) \mid y \in A\}$.

nodes.name: Strict separation by a linear map
nodes.statement:
Suppose also that $Y$ is Dedekind complete.
We say that \emph {$f$ strictly separates $x$ from $A$} if $f$ separates $x$ from $A$ and
the appropriate condition is strengthened as either $f (x) < \inf f (A)$ or $f (x) > \sup f (A)$.

nodes.name: $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces, $Y$ is Dedekind complete and $\mathcal L$ is a linear subspace of $\linop {X} {Y}$. We say that $X$ satisfies the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property if for any $x, y \in X_+$ and $z \in [0, x + y] \setminus ([0, x] + [0, y])$ point $z$ cannot be strictly separated from $[0, x] + [0, y]$ by a map from $\mathcal L$.
nodes.statement_short: Points of $[0,x+y]$ outside $[0,x]+[0,y]$ cannot be strictly separated from it by maps in $\mathcal L$.
nodes.label: wrdp

nodes.name: Riesz Decomposition Property implies L-Riesz Decomposition Property
nodes.statement:
Trivially, if $X$ satisfies the Riesz Decomposition Property then it satisfies the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property with any
$\mathcal L$.
assumptions: $X$ satisfies the Riesz Decomposition Property
conclusions: it satisfies the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property with any $\mathcal L$

nodes.name: Order in R^3 with L-RDP but without RDP
nodes.statement:
On the other hand, however, it is easy to construct an example that shows that the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property
is weaker than
the Riesz Decomposition Property for $Y = \mathbb R$ and the widest possible space $\mathcal L = \linop {X} {\mathbb R}$.
We will now give a detailed description of such an example; see Figure~\ref {figrdpex}.
\begin{figure} [tbph]
\includegraphics [width=13cm] {rdp.pdf}
\caption {Order intervals in an example of an order in $\mathbb R^3$ that satisfies the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property but does not satisfy the
Riesz Decomposition Property.
The order intervals $[0, (2, 1, 1)]$ and $[0, (1, 2, 1)]$ (top row) sum up to $[0, (2, 1, 1)] + [0, (1, 2, 1)]$ (bottom right); however,
the order interval $[0, (2, 1, 1) + (1, 2, 1)] = [0, (3, 3, 2)]$ (bottom left) has longer segments on the boundary.
} \end{figure}
Let
$X = \mathbb R^3$
and

 






 
$X_+ = \{ (x, y, z) \mid \text {$x, y, z > 0$ or $z = 0$, $x = y \geqslant 0$}\}$.
Observe that order interval $[0, (2, 1, 1)]$ is the union of an open rectangular box
$
\{(x, y, z) \mid 0 < x < 2, \,\, 0 < y < 1, \,\, 0 < z < 1\}
$
and two parallel semiopen segments connecting $(0, 0, 0)$ with $(1, 1, 0)$ not including $(1, 1, 0)$ 
and $(2, 1, 1)$ with $(1, 0, 1)$ not including $(1, 0, 1)$.  The order interval $[0, (1, 2, 1)]$ has similar structure because
it is the mirror image of $[0, (2, 1, 1)]$ with respect to the symmetry plane $\{(x, y, z) \mid x = y \}$ of $X_+$.  It is easy to see that
$
[0, (2, 1, 1) + (1, 2, 1)] = [0, (3, 3, 2)]
$
is the union of an open rectangular box
$$
\{(x, y, z) \mid 0 < x < 3, \,\, 0 < y < 3, \,\, 0 < z < 2\}
$$
and two parallel semiopen segments connecting $(0, 0, 0)$ with $(3, 3, 0)$ not including $(3, 3, 0)$ and
$(3, 3, 2)$ with $(0, 0, 2)$ not including $(0, 0, 2)$.  Thus
$[0, (3, 3, 2)] \setminus \left([0, (2, 1, 1)] + [0, (1, 2, 1)]\right)$ is a union of a semiopen segment between $(0, 0, 3)$ and $(1, 1, 3)$
not including $(0, 0, 3)$
and a semiopen segment between $(2, 2, 0)$ and $(3, 3, 0)$ not including $(3, 3, 0)$, and so
$X$ does not satisfy the Riesz Decomposition Property.  However, observe that the closure of the order intervals $[0, a]$, $a \in X_+$
(in the standard topology of $\mathbb R^3$, which is the only topology there is that turns $\mathbb R^3$ into a Hausdorff linear topological space)
coincides with the order intervals of $\mathbb R^3$ ordered by the standard cone
$$
\mathbb R^3_+ = \{(x, y, z) \mid x \geqslant 0, \,\, y \geqslant 0, \,\, z \geqslant 0 \}
$$
with which $\mathbb R^3$
is a lattice and thus has
the Riesz Decomposition Property.  Therefore for all $a, b \in X_+$ the set $[0, a + b] \setminus \left([0, a] + [0, b]\right)$ lies in the closure
of $[0, a + b]$.
Since $X$ is finite dimensional,
every functional from $\mathcal L$
is continuous and therefore cannot strictly separate a convex set from a point in its closure.  Thus
$X$ satisfies the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property for any $\mathcal L$.
nodes.statement_short: A non-closed cone in $\mathbb R^3$ whose order intervals fail RDP only on boundary segments, so continuous functionals cannot strictly separate: L-RDP holds, RDP fails.

nodes.name: L-RDP for small operator spaces
nodes.statement:
Of course, if the set $\mathcal L$ is very small with respect to $\linop {X} {Y}$ in a certain sense, for example if $X$ is infinite-dimensional
and all operators from $\mathcal L$ factor through a finite-dimensional space, then the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property
may be \emph {much} more general than the Riesz Decomposition Property; an obvious example is that \emph {any} couple of ordered linear spaces
$X$, $Y$ satisfies the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property if all operators from $\mathcal L$ factor through a one-dimensional space,
or just $\mathcal L = \{0\}$.
nodes.statement_short: If all maps in $\mathcal L$ factor through low-dimensional spaces, L-RDP is much weaker than RDP; trivially true for $\mathcal L=\{0\}$.

nodes.name: RDP equals C(X,R)-RDP for compact order intervals
nodes.statement: Suppose that ordered linear space $X$ is equipped with a topology that turns it into a locally convex Hausdorff linear space and order intervals $[0, x]$ are compact for any $x \in X_+$. Then $X$ satisfies the Riesz Decomposition Property if and only if $X$ satisfies the $\clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$-Riesz Decomposition Property.
assumptions: ordered linear space $X$ is equipped with a topology that turns it into a locally convex Hausdorff linear space
order intervals $[0, x]$ are compact for any $x \in X_+$
conclusions: $X$ satisfies the Riesz Decomposition Property if and only if $X$ satisfies the $\clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$-Riesz Decomposition Property
nodes.label: rdplrdp

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2
nodes.statement:
Indeed, suppose that $X$ satisfies the $\clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$-Riesz Decomposition Property under the conditions of Proposition~\ref {rdplrdp}
and there exist some $x, y \in X_+$ and $z \in [0, x + y] \setminus \left( [0, x] + [0, y] \right)$.
$[0, x] + [0, y]$ is a compact convex set because it is the Minkowski sum of two compact convex sets.  Then by a standard separation theorem
$z$ can be strictly separated from $[0, x] + [0, y]$ by some $f \in \clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$, a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction: a point outside the compact convex sum $[0,x]+[0,y]$ is strictly separated from it by a continuous functional.

nodes.name: Contradiction hypothesis
nodes.statement:
Indeed, suppose that $X$ satisfies the $\clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$-Riesz Decomposition Property under the conditions of Proposition~\ref {rdplrdp}
and there exist some $x, y \in X_+$ and $z \in [0, x + y] \setminus \left( [0, x] + [0, y] \right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $\mathcal C$-RDP and a point $z$ violating RDP

nodes.name: Strict separation
nodes.statement:
$[0, x] + [0, y]$ is a compact convex set because it is the Minkowski sum of two compact convex sets.  Then by a standard separation theorem
$z$ can be strictly separated from $[0, x] + [0, y]$ by some $f \in \clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$, a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Compactness of the Minkowski sum plus strict separation gives a contradiction

nodes.name: Base of a cone
nodes.statement:
Suppose that $X$ is an ordered linear space and $B \subset X$ is a convex set.
We say that a cone $X_+$ \emph {has a base $B$} if for any $x \in X_+ \setminus \{0\}$
there exist unique $y \in B$ and $\lambda > 0$ such that $x = \lambda y$;
for details on cones with bases see, e.~g., \cite [Section~1.7] {conesandduality}.

nodes.name: Bases and strictly positive functionals
nodes.statement:
Existence of a base for $X_+$ is equiuvalent to existence of a strictly positive functional $f$ in $X$; in this case the set
$B = \{ x \in X_+ \mid f (x) = 1\}$ is a base for $X_+$.
conclusions: Existence of a base for $X_+$ is equiuvalent to existence of a strictly positive functional $f$ in $X$
the set $B = \{ x \in X_+ \mid f (x) = 1\}$ is a base for $X_+$
equivalent_conditions: existence of a strictly positive functional $f$ in $X$

nodes.name: Restrictions to a base
nodes.statement:
Restrictions of maps from $\linop {X} {Y}$ on $B$ are exactly the affine functionals on $B$ taking values in $Y$, and restrictions
$K \cap B$ of convex cones $K \subset X_+$ are exactly the convex subsets of $B$.
conclusions: Restrictions of maps from $\linop {X} {Y}$ on $B$ are exactly the affine functionals on $B$ taking values in $Y$
restrictions $K \cap B$ of convex cones $K \subset X_+$ are exactly the convex subsets of $B$

nodes.name: Bounded aperture on parallel lines
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be an ordered linear space such that the cone $X_+$ has a base $B$. We say that $X_+$ has bounded aperture on parallel lines if for any $x \in X$ there exists some $c_x \geqslant 0$ such that for any $y \in B \setminus \{x\}$ the length of the intersection $B \cap \ell$ is at most $c_x$, where $\ell$ is the line passing through points $y$ and $x + y$.
nodes.statement_short: Every family of parallel chords of the base in a given direction has uniformly bounded length.
nodes.label: finap

nodes.name: Only affine-hull directions matter
nodes.statement:
It is sufficient to consider only points $x$ from the affine hull of $B$ in Definition~\ref {finap},
since otherwise $B \cap \ell$ is a single point.

nodes.name: Bounded aperture is independent of the base
nodes.statement:
Also, since all bases of a cone are affinely isomorphic
and affine maps preserve relative lengths of parallel segments, Definition~\ref {finap} does not depend on a particular choice of a base $B$.

nodes.name: Bounded aperture in finite dimensions
nodes.statement:
It is easy to see that for the finite dimensional ordered spaces the cone $X_+$ has bounded aperture if and only if its closure
does not contain any lines, i.~e. one-dimensional spaces.
assumptions: for the finite dimensional ordered spaces
conclusions: the cone $X_+$ has bounded aperture if and only if its closure does not contain any lines
equivalent_conditions: its closure does not contain any lines

nodes.name: Compact base implies bounded aperture
nodes.statement:
It is also easy to see that if $X$ is a Hausdorff ordered linear topological space such that the cone $X_+$ has a compact base $B$ then
the cone $X_+$ has bounded aperture on parallel lines; however, this property seems to be much weaker than any kind of compactness.
assumptions: $X$ is a Hausdorff ordered linear topological space such that the cone $X_+$ has a compact base $B$
conclusions: the cone $X_+$ has bounded aperture on parallel lines

nodes.name: Bounded convex base in a normed space
nodes.statement:
For example, if $B$ is a bounded convex set in an infinite dimensional
normed linear space then the cone $X_+$ has bounded aperture on parallel lines (since the length of $B \cap \ell$ in Definition~\ref {finap}
is proportional to $\|z_0 - z_1\|$, where $z_0$ and $z_1$ are the endpoints of $B \cap \ell$),
but at the same time $B$ may lack any meaningful kind of compactness.

nodes.name: Separation of cones by a regular functional
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ is an ordered linear space such that the cone $X_+$ is generating for $X$ and $X_+$ has bounded aperture on parallel lines. Let $K_0, K_1 \subset X_+$ be two nonempty convex cones such that $K_0 \cap K_1 = \emptyset$ and $\mathrm{int} K_0 \neq \emptyset$. Then there exists a regular functional $f \in \rlinop {X} {\mathbb R}$, $f \neq 0$, such that $f$ separates $K_0$ and $K_1$.
assumptions: $X$ is an ordered linear space such that the cone $X_+$ is generating for $X$
$X_+$ has bounded aperture on parallel lines
$K_0, K_1 \subset X_+$ be two nonempty convex cones such that $K_0 \cap K_1 = \emptyset$
$\mathrm{int} K_0 \neq \emptyset$
conclusions: there exists a regular functional $f \in \rlinop {X} {\mathbb R}$, $f \neq 0$, such that $f$ separates $K_0$ and $K_1$
nodes.label: regfuncsep

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4
nodes.statement:
Indeed, let $B$ be a base of the cone $X_+$, let $L$ be the affine hull of $B$ and let $A_j = K_j \cap B$ for $j \in \{0, 1\}$.
Then $\mathrm{int} A_0 \neq \emptyset$ as a subset of $L$ (for the rest of the proof we denote by $\mathrm{int} D$ the sets of internal points of
$D \subset L$ in $L$ rather than in $X$),
and by the standard separation theorem there exists a linear functional
$h_{00} \in \linop {L} {\mathbb R}$ separating $A_0$ and $A_1$.  This means that for some $\alpha \in \mathbb R$ the hyperplane
$H = \{y \in L \mid h_{00} (y) = \alpha\}$ separates $A_0$ and $A_1$ in $L$.
Let $x_0 \in \mathrm{int} A_0$ and let $y_0 \in H \cap B$; then $x_0 \notin H$.  Space $L$ can then be parametrized as
$L = \{s (x_0 - y_0) + y \mid s \in \mathbb R, y \in H \}$.
By the bounded aperture property assumption there exists some $c \in \mathbb R$ such that
\begin{equation} B \subset \{s (x_0 - y_0) + y \mid |s| \leqslant c, \,\, y \in H \}.
\end{equation}
Let us define two affine functionals for $z = s (x_0 - y_0) + y$, $s \in \mathbb R$, $y \in H$ by
$h_0 (z) = 1 + \frac 1 {2 c} s$ and $h_1 (z) = 1 - \frac 1 {2 c} s$, and let $f_0, f_1 \in \linop {X} {\mathbb R}$
be the unique linear extensions of $h_0$ and $h_1$.
\eqref {positiveonb} implies that $h_0$ and $h_1$ are positive on $B$, so we have $f_0, f_1 \geqslant 0$ and thus $f = f_0 - f_1$
is a regular functional that is a unique extension of $h = h_0 - h_1$.  By construction $h$ is an affine functional that defines the same hyperplane
$H$, i.~e. $H = \{y \in L \mid h (y) = 0 \}$, and it is easy to see that we also have $h (A_0) \leqslant 0$ and $h (A_1) \geqslant 0$,
so $h$ separates $A_0$ and $A_1$, and therefore $f$ separates $K_0$ and $K_1$.  The proof of Proposition~\ref {regfuncsep} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Separate the traces on a base by a hyperplane, then use bounded aperture to write the separating functional as a difference of two positive ones.

nodes.name: Restrict to the base
nodes.statement: Indeed, let $B$ be a base of the cone $X_+$, let $L$ be the affine hull of $B$ and let $A_j = K_j \cap B$ for $j \in \{0, 1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Pass to the base $B$ and its affine hull $L$

nodes.name: Separating hyperplane
nodes.statement:
Then $\mathrm{int} A_0 \neq \emptyset$ as a subset of $L$ (for the rest of the proof we denote by $\mathrm{int} D$ the sets of internal points of
$D \subset L$ in $L$ rather than in $X$),
and by the standard separation theorem there exists a linear functional
$h_{00} \in \linop {L} {\mathbb R}$ separating $A_0$ and $A_1$.  This means that for some $\alpha \in \mathbb R$ the hyperplane
$H = \{y \in L \mid h_{00} (y) = \alpha\}$ separates $A_0$ and $A_1$ in $L$.
nodes.statement_short: Standard separation theorem gives a separating hyperplane $H$ in $L$

nodes.name: Parametrization of L
nodes.statement:
Let $x_0 \in \mathrm{int} A_0$ and let $y_0 \in H \cap B$; then $x_0 \notin H$.  Space $L$ can then be parametrized as
$L = \{s (x_0 - y_0) + y \mid s \in \mathbb R, y \in H \}$.
nodes.statement_short: Parametrize $L$ transversally to $H$

nodes.name: Slab bound
nodes.statement_short: Bounded aperture confines $B$ to a slab $|s| \le c$

nodes.name: Affine functionals h_0, h_1
nodes.statement:
Let us define two affine functionals for $z = s (x_0 - y_0) + y$, $s \in \mathbb R$, $y \in H$ by
$h_0 (z) = 1 + \frac 1 {2 c} s$ and $h_1 (z) = 1 - \frac 1 {2 c} s$, and let $f_0, f_1 \in \linop {X} {\mathbb R}$
be the unique linear extensions of $h_0$ and $h_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Define two affine functionals and their linear extensions

nodes.name: Regular separating functional
nodes.statement:
\eqref {positiveonb} implies that $h_0$ and $h_1$ are positive on $B$, so we have $f_0, f_1 \geqslant 0$ and thus $f = f_0 - f_1$
is a regular functional that is a unique extension of $h = h_0 - h_1$.  By construction $h$ is an affine functional that defines the same hyperplane
$H$, i.~e. $H = \{y \in L \mid h (y) = 0 \}$, and it is easy to see that we also have $h (A_0) \leqslant 0$ and $h (A_1) \geqslant 0$,
so $h$ separates $A_0$ and $A_1$, and therefore $f$ separates $K_0$ and $K_1$.  The proof of Proposition~\ref {regfuncsep} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Their difference is a regular functional defining $H$, hence separating $K_0$ and $K_1$

nodes.name: Slab containing the base
nodes.statement: B \subset \{s (x_0 - y_0) + y \mid |s| \leqslant c, \,\, y \in H \}.
nodes.label: positiveonb

nodes.name: Bounded aperture cannot be dropped
nodes.statement:
It is not difficult to see that the assumption that $X_+$ has bounded aperture on parallel lines cannot be dropped
from Proposition~\ref {regfuncsep}: if the affine hull of the base $B$ of $X_+$ contains a line $\ell$,
then any positive functional $f_0$ has to be constant on $\ell$, and thus no
$f \in \rlinop {X} {\mathbb R}$, $f \neq 0$, can separate any cones $K_0, K_1 \subset X_+$ such that $\ell \cap \mathrm{int} K_j \neq \emptyset$ for $j \in \{0, 1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: If the affine hull of the base contains a line, positive functionals are constant on it, so no nonzero regular functional separates such cones.

nodes.name: Hyperplanes defined by regular functionals
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ is an ordered linear space such that the cone $X_+$ is generating in $X$, $X_+$ has bounded aperture on parallel lines and $\mathrm{int} X_+ \neq \emptyset$. Let $H \subset X$ be a hyperplane. Then there exists a regular functional $f \in \rlinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ such that $H = \{x \mid f (x) = \alpha\}$ with some $\alpha \in \mathbb R$.
assumptions: $X$ is an ordered linear space such that the cone $X_+$ is generating in $X$
$X_+$ has bounded aperture on parallel lines
$\mathrm{int} X_+ \neq \emptyset$
$H \subset X$ be a hyperplane
conclusions: there exists a regular functional $f \in \rlinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ such that $H = \{x \mid f (x) = \alpha\}$ with some $\alpha \in \mathbb R$
nodes.label: regfunchp

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5
nodes.statement:
First, fix any $x_0 \in H$, and let $H_0 = H - x_0$; we want to find some
$f \in \rlinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ such that $H_0 = \{x \mid f (x) = 0\}$.
Let $h_0 \in \linop {X} {\mathbb R}$ be a (not necessarily regular) linear functional defining $H_0$,
that is $H_0 = \{x \mid h_0 (x) = 0\}$.
If $H_0 \cap X_+ = \{0\}$ then either $h_0$ or $-h_0$ is positive and we can put $f = h_0$ right away.
Otherwise let
$$
K_0 = \{x \in X_+ \mid h_0 (x) < 0\}
$$
and
$$
K_1 = \{x \in X_+ \mid h_0 (x) > 0\}.
$$
By assumptions there exists some $z \in \mathrm{int} X_+$.  We may assume that $z \notin H_0$, since otherwise we may replace $z$ with a convex combination
of $z$ and some point in $X_+ \setminus H_0$ (we cannot have $X_+ \subset H_0$ since $X_+$ is assumed to be generating in $X$).
Therefore
$$
z \in K_j = \{h_0 < 0\} \cap \mathrm{int} X_+ = \mathrm{int} K_j
$$
for some $j \in \{0, 1\}$;
by changing the sign of $h_0$ we may thus assume that $\mathrm{int} K_0 \neq \emptyset$.
Applying Proposition~\ref {regfuncsep} yields a functional $f_0 \in \rlinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ separating $K_0$ and $K_1$,
and since the cone $X_+$ is generating in $X$, it is easy to see that $H_0 = \{ x \mid f (x) = 0\}$.
Finally, $H = \{x \mid f (x) = f (x_0)\}$, and the proof of Proposition~\ref {regfunchp} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Translate to a linear hyperplane; if it meets the cone only at 0 its functional is positive, otherwise separate the two open half-cones by Proposition 4.

nodes.name: Reduction to a linear hyperplane
nodes.statement:
First, fix any $x_0 \in H$, and let $H_0 = H - x_0$; we want to find some
$f \in \rlinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ such that $H_0 = \{x \mid f (x) = 0\}$.
Let $h_0 \in \linop {X} {\mathbb R}$ be a (not necessarily regular) linear functional defining $H_0$,
that is $H_0 = \{x \mid h_0 (x) = 0\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the linear hyperplane $H_0$ with defining functional $h_0$

nodes.name: Trivial case
nodes.statement: If $H_0 \cap X_+ = \{0\}$ then either $h_0$ or $-h_0$ is positive and we can put $f = h_0$ right away.
nodes.statement_short: Case $H_0 \cap X_+ = \{0\}$: $\pm h_0$ is positive

nodes.name: General case
nodes.statement:
Otherwise let
$$
K_0 = \{x \in X_+ \mid h_0 (x) < 0\}
$$
and
$$
K_1 = \{x \in X_+ \mid h_0 (x) > 0\}.
$$
By assumptions there exists some $z \in \mathrm{int} X_+$.  We may assume that $z \notin H_0$, since otherwise we may replace $z$ with a convex combination
of $z$ and some point in $X_+ \setminus H_0$ (we cannot have $X_+ \subset H_0$ since $X_+$ is assumed to be generating in $X$).
Therefore
$$
z \in K_j = \{h_0 < 0\} \cap \mathrm{int} X_+ = \mathrm{int} K_j
$$
for some $j \in \{0, 1\}$;
by changing the sign of $h_0$ we may thus assume that $\mathrm{int} K_0 \neq \emptyset$.
Applying Proposition~\ref {regfuncsep} yields a functional $f_0 \in \rlinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ separating $K_0$ and $K_1$,
and since the cone $X_+$ is generating in $X$, it is easy to see that $H_0 = \{ x \mid f (x) = 0\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise separate the two half-cones of $X_+$

nodes.name: Half-cones
nodes.statement:
Otherwise let
$$
K_0 = \{x \in X_+ \mid h_0 (x) < 0\}
$$
and
$$
K_1 = \{x \in X_+ \mid h_0 (x) > 0\}.
$$
nodes.statement_short: Define the open half-cones $K_0$, $K_1$

nodes.name: Interior of a half-cone
nodes.statement:
By assumptions there exists some $z \in \mathrm{int} X_+$.  We may assume that $z \notin H_0$, since otherwise we may replace $z$ with a convex combination
of $z$ and some point in $X_+ \setminus H_0$ (we cannot have $X_+ \subset H_0$ since $X_+$ is assumed to be generating in $X$).
Therefore
$$
z \in K_j = \{h_0 < 0\} \cap \mathrm{int} X_+ = \mathrm{int} K_j
$$
for some $j \in \{0, 1\}$;
by changing the sign of $h_0$ we may thus assume that $\mathrm{int} K_0 \neq \emptyset$.
nodes.statement_short: An internal point off $H_0$ shows one half-cone has internal points

nodes.name: Apply separation
nodes.statement:
Applying Proposition~\ref {regfuncsep} yields a functional $f_0 \in \rlinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ separating $K_0$ and $K_1$,
and since the cone $X_+$ is generating in $X$, it is easy to see that $H_0 = \{ x \mid f (x) = 0\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Proposition 4 to get a regular functional vanishing on $H_0$

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Finally, $H = \{x \mid f (x) = f (x_0)\}$, and the proof of Proposition~\ref {regfunchp} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Translate back to $H$

nodes.name: Difference of nested line-open convex sets
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ is a linear space and $B \subset A \subset X$ are nonempty, convex and line-open, i.~e. $A = \mathrm{int} A$ and $B = \mathrm{int} B$. Then $A \setminus B \neq \emptyset$ implies that $\mathrm{int} (A \setminus B) \neq \emptyset$; moreover, \begin{equation} A \cap \{z \mid g (z) > \alpha\} \subset \mathrm{int} (A \setminus B) \end{equation} for some $g \in \linop {X} {\mathbb R}$ and $\alpha \in \mathbb R$.
assumptions: $X$ is a linear space
$B \subset A \subset X$ are nonempty, convex and line-open
conclusions: $A \setminus B \neq \emptyset$ implies that $\mathrm{int} (A \setminus B) \neq \emptyset$
A \cap \{z \mid g (z) > \alpha\} \subset \mathrm{int} (A \setminus B)
nodes.label: aocsd

nodes.name: Open half-space inside the difference
nodes.statement: A \cap \{z \mid g (z) > \alpha\} \subset \mathrm{int} (A \setminus B)
nodes.label: aseplf

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 6
nodes.statement:
Indeed, let $y_0 \in A \setminus B$ and $x_0 \in \mathrm{int} B$.  By the standard separation theorem there exists a hyperplane
$H = \{ y \mid g (y) = \alpha\}$ separating $y_0$ and $B$.  By changing the sign of $g$ if necessary we may assume that $g (x_0) < \alpha$ and
$g (y_0) \geqslant \alpha$.
Since $A$ is line-open, there exists some $\lambda > 1$
such that $y = x_0 + \lambda (y_0 - x_0) \in A$.  Therefore $g (y) = g (y_0) + (\lambda  - 1) (g (y_0) - g (x_0))  > \alpha$.
This means that $y$ belongs to the line-open set \eqref {aseplf}.
nodes.statement_short: Separate a point of $A\setminus B$ from $B$ by a hyperplane and push past it along a line inside line-open $A$.

nodes.name: Separating hyperplane
nodes.statement:
Indeed, let $y_0 \in A \setminus B$ and $x_0 \in \mathrm{int} B$.  By the standard separation theorem there exists a hyperplane
$H = \{ y \mid g (y) = \alpha\}$ separating $y_0$ and $B$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick points and separate $y_0$ from $B$ by a hyperplane

nodes.name: Sign normalization
nodes.statement:
By changing the sign of $g$ if necessary we may assume that $g (x_0) < \alpha$ and
$g (y_0) \geqslant \alpha$.
nodes.statement_short: Normalize the sign of $g$

nodes.name: Point beyond the hyperplane
nodes.statement:
Since $A$ is line-open, there exists some $\lambda > 1$
such that $y = x_0 + \lambda (y_0 - x_0) \in A$.  Therefore $g (y) = g (y_0) + (\lambda  - 1) (g (y_0) - g (x_0))  > \alpha$.
nodes.statement_short: Line-openness gives a point of $A$ strictly beyond $H$

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: This means that $y$ belongs to the line-open set \eqref {aseplf}.
nodes.statement_short: That point lies in the open set (aseplf)

nodes.name: RDP equals L-RDP for line-open cones
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ is an ordered linear space satisfying $X_+ = \{0\} \cup \mathrm{int} X_+$, the cone $X_+$ is generating for $X$, $X_+$ has bounded aperture on parallel lines and $Y$ is an ordered linear space such that the cone $Y_+$ is generating for $Y$. Let $\mathcal L \subset \linop {X} {Y}$ be a linear space of linear maps such that $y_0 \cdot \rlinop {X} {\mathbb R} \subset \mathcal L$ for some $y_0 \in Y$. Then the following conditions are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item $X$ has the Riesz Decomposition Property. \item $X$ has the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: $X$ is an ordered linear space satisfying $X_+ = \{0\} \cup \mathrm{int} X_+$
the cone $X_+$ is generating for $X$
$X_+$ has bounded aperture on parallel lines
$Y$ is an ordered linear space such that the cone $Y_+$ is generating for $Y$
$\mathcal L \subset \linop {X} {Y}$ be a linear space of linear maps such that $y_0 \cdot \rlinop {X} {\mathbb R} \subset \mathcal L$ for some $y_0 \in Y$
conclusions: the following conditions are equivalent.
nodes.statement_short: For line-open cones with bounded aperture, RDP and $\mathcal L$-RDP coincide whenever $\mathcal L$ contains $y_0$ times the regular functionals.
nodes.label: openlrdp

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 7
nodes.statement:
Indeed, $1 \Rightarrow 2$ is trivial and so we only need to establish $2 \Rightarrow 1$.
It is easy to see that we may, without loss of generality, assume that $Y = \mathbb R$ and $\rlinop {X} {\mathbb R} \subset \mathcal L$
under the conditions of Proposition~\ref {openlrdp}.
Suppose that $X$ has the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property but there exist some $x, y, z \in X_+$
such that
$z \in [0, x + y] \setminus \left([0, x] + [0, y]\right)$.
Since by the assumptions $X_+ = \{0\} \cup \mathrm{int} X_+$, we have $[0, x] = \{0\} \cup \mathrm{int} [0, x]$ and thus
$[0, x] + [0, y] = \{0\} \cup \mathrm{int} \left( [0, x] + [0, y]\right)$.
It is easy to see that $\mathrm{int} [0, x] \neq \emptyset$ unless $X$ is trivial.
Let $x_0 \in [0, x] + [0, y]$.
Using Proposition~\ref {aocsd}, we may assume that
\begin{equation} z \in A = \mathrm{int} \left( [0, x + y] \setminus \left([0, x] + [0, y]\right) \right) \subset [0, x + y] \cap \{z \mid g (z) > \alpha\}
\end{equation}
with some linear functional $g$.
Let $H = \{z \mid g (z) = \alpha\}$.
Then by Proposition~\ref {regfunchp} there exists a regular functional $f \in \rlinop {X} {\mathbb R}$
such that
$
H = \{a \mid f (a) = \beta\}
$
with some $\beta \in \mathbb R$.
This means that $f$ separates $A$ and $[0, x] + [0, y]$, and therefore strictly separates
$z \in A = \mathrm{int} A$ from $[0, x] + [0, y]$, which contradicts the assumption that
$X$ satisfies the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property.  The proof of Theorem~\ref {openlrdp} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction: by Proposition 6 a bad point lies in an open set cut off by a hyperplane, which Proposition 5 realizes by a regular functional that strictly separates it.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement:
Indeed, $1 \Rightarrow 2$ is trivial and so we only need to establish $2 \Rightarrow 1$.
It is easy to see that we may, without loss of generality, assume that $Y = \mathbb R$ and $\rlinop {X} {\mathbb R} \subset \mathcal L$
under the conditions of Proposition~\ref {openlrdp}.
nodes.statement_short: Only $2\Rightarrow1$ needs proof; reduce WLOG to $Y=\mathbb R$

nodes.name: Contradiction hypothesis
nodes.statement:
Suppose that $X$ has the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property but there exist some $x, y, z \in X_+$
such that
$z \in [0, x + y] \setminus \left([0, x] + [0, y]\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume L-RDP holds but RDP fails at $z$

nodes.name: Line-openness of intervals
nodes.statement:
Since by the assumptions $X_+ = \{0\} \cup \mathrm{int} X_+$, we have $[0, x] = \{0\} \cup \mathrm{int} [0, x]$ and thus
$[0, x] + [0, y] = \{0\} \cup \mathrm{int} \left( [0, x] + [0, y]\right)$.
It is easy to see that $\mathrm{int} [0, x] \neq \emptyset$ unless $X$ is trivial.
nodes.statement_short: Order intervals and their sums are line-open up to $0$

nodes.name: Apply Proposition 6
nodes.statement_short: By Proposition 6 place $z$ in an open set cut off by a functional $g$

nodes.name: Apply Proposition 5
nodes.statement:
Let $H = \{z \mid g (z) = \alpha\}$.
Then by Proposition~\ref {regfunchp} there exists a regular functional $f \in \rlinop {X} {\mathbb R}$
such that
$
H = \{a \mid f (a) = \beta\}
$
with some $\beta \in \mathbb R$.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 5 realizes the hyperplane by a regular functional $f$

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement:
This means that $f$ separates $A$ and $[0, x] + [0, y]$, and therefore strictly separates
$z \in A = \mathrm{int} A$ from $[0, x] + [0, y]$, which contradicts the assumption that
$X$ satisfies the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property.  The proof of Theorem~\ref {openlrdp} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: $f$ strictly separates $z$, contradicting L-RDP

nodes.name: Location of the bad point
nodes.statement: z \in A = \mathrm{int} \left( [0, x + y] \setminus \left([0, x] + [0, y]\right) \right) \subset [0, x + y] \cap \{z \mid g (z) > \alpha\}
nodes.label: ztint

nodes.name: Riesz-Kantorovich transform
nodes.statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be ordered linear spaces, $n \geqslant 1$ and $T = \left\{T_1, \ldots, T_n\right\}$ be a finite collection of superlinear maps $T_j : X_+ \to Y$ for $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$. The Riesz-Kantorovich transform $$ \rkts {T} = \rkts {T_1, \ldots, T_n} : x \mapsto \rkt {T} {x} $$ is defined by \begin{multline} \rkt {T} {x} = \rkt {T_1, \ldots, T_n} {x} = \\ \sup \left\{ \sum_{j = 1}^n T_j (x_j) \mid x_j \in X_+ \text { for $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$ and } \sum_{j = 1}^n x_j \leqslant x \right\} \end{multline} for $x \in X_+$ whenever this supremum exists in $Y$. The positive Riesz-Kantorovich transform is defined by $$ \rktp {T} {x} = \rktp {T_1, \ldots, T_n} {x} = \rktp {0, T_1, \ldots, T_n} {x}. $$
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal R(T)(x)$ is the sup of $\sum T_j(x_j)$ over positive decompositions $\sum x_j \le x$; the positive transform adds the zero map.
nodes.label: rktd

nodes.name: Definition of the Riesz-Kantorovich transform
nodes.statement: \rkt {T} {x} = \rkt {T_1, \ldots, T_n} {x} = \\ \sup \left\{ \sum_{j = 1}^n T_j (x_j) \mid x_j \in X_+ \text { for $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$ and } \sum_{j = 1}^n x_j \leqslant x \right\}
nodes.label: rktdef

nodes.name: Well-definedness of the Riesz-Kantorovich transform
nodes.statement:
It is easy to see that if maps $T_j$ are order bounded and $Y$ is Dedekind complete then the Riesz-Kantorovich transform $\rkt {T} {x}$ is well-defined
and $\rkts {T_1, \ldots, T_n} \geqslant T_j$ for all $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$.
assumptions: maps $T_j$ are order bounded
$Y$ is Dedekind complete
conclusions: the Riesz-Kantorovich transform $\rkt {T} {x}$ is well-defined
$\rkts {T_1, \ldots, T_n} \geqslant T_j$ for all $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$

nodes.name: The Riesz-Kantorovich transform is superlinear
nodes.statement:
Since
$[0, x] + [0, y] \subset [0, x + y]$ for all $x, y \in X_+$, it is easy to verify that $\rkts {T}$ is superadditive.
Since the Riesz-Kantorovich transform is also positively homogeneous,
we see that $\rkts {T}$ is a superlinear map that majorizes $T_j$ for all $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$.
conclusions: $\rkts {T}$ is superadditive
$\rkts {T}$ is a superlinear map that majorizes $T_j$ for all $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$

nodes.name: The Riesz-Kantorovich transform is order bounded
nodes.statement:
Observe also that
$\rkts {T}$ is order bounded whenever the operators from collection $T$ are.
assumptions: the operators from collection $T$ are
conclusions: $\rkts {T}$ is order bounded

nodes.name: Riesz-Kantorovich transform is the least superlinear majorant
nodes.statement: Suppose that under the assumptions of Definition~\ref {rktd} map $\rkts {T}$ is well-defined. Then \begin{multline} \rkts {T} = \\ \inf \{S : X_+ \to Y \mid \text {$S$ is superlinear and $S \geqslant T_j$ for all $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$}\}. \end{multline} In particular, $\rkts {T} = \bigvee_{j = 1}^n T_j$ in \suplinop {X_+} {Y}.
assumptions: under the assumptions of Definition~\ref {rktd} map $\rkts {T}$ is well-defined
conclusions: \rkts {T} = \\ \inf \{S : X_+ \to Y \mid \text {$S$ is superlinear and $S \geqslant T_j$ for all $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$}\}.
$\rkts {T} = \bigvee_{j = 1}^n T_j$ in \suplinop {X_+} {Y}
nodes.statement_short: When defined, the RK transform is the infimum of superlinear majorants, i.e. the supremum of the $T_j$ among superlinear maps.
nodes.label: rktinf

nodes.name: RK transform as infimum of superlinear majorants
nodes.statement: \rkts {T} = \\ \inf \{S : X_+ \to Y \mid \text {$S$ is superlinear and $S \geqslant T_j$ for all $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$}\}.
nodes.label: rktinfrel

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 9
nodes.statement_short: Any superlinear majorant $S$ dominates every sum $\sum T_j(x_j)$ by superadditivity, hence dominates the RK transform.

nodes.name: Superadditivity bound for a superlinear majorant
nodes.statement: S (x) \geqslant \sum_{j = 1}^n S (x_j) \geqslant \sum_{j = 1}^n T_j (x_j)
nodes.label: sssup

nodes.name: Associativity of the Riesz-Kantorovich transform
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces and $Y$ is Dedekind complete. Then for any order bounded superlinear maps $Q, R, S : X \to Y$ we have the relations \begin{equation} \rkts {\rkts {Q, R}, S} = \rkts {Q, R, S} = \rkts {Q, \rkts {R, S}}. \end{equation}
assumptions: $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces and $Y$ is Dedekind complete
for any order bounded superlinear maps $Q, R, S : X \to Y$
conclusions: \rkts {\rkts {Q, R}, S} = \rkts {Q, R, S} = \rkts {Q, \rkts {R, S}}.
nodes.label: rkass

nodes.name: Associativity relations
nodes.statement: \rkts {\rkts {Q, R}, S} = \rkts {Q, R, S} = \rkts {Q, \rkts {R, S}}.
nodes.label: asseq

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 10
nodes.statement:
By symmetry it is sufficient to establish the first equality in \eqref {asseq}.
Observe that \eqref {rktinfrel} implies that $\rkts {Q, R, S} \geqslant \rkts {Q, R}$, and another application of Proposition~\ref {rktinf}
yields $\rkts {Q, R, S} \geqslant \rkts {\rkts {Q, R}, S}$.
Let us verify the converse inequality.  Suppose that $w \in X_+$.  Then for any $x, y, z \in X_+$ such that $x + y + z \leqslant w$
we have
$$
\rkt {\rkts {Q, R}, S} {w} \geqslant \rkt {Q, R} {x + y} + S (z) \geqslant Q (x) + R (y) + S (z),
$$
so $\rkts {\rkts {Q, R}, S} \geqslant \rkts {Q, R, S}$.
nodes.statement_short: One inequality from minimality (Proposition 9), the other by splitting a decomposition $x+y+z \le w$.

nodes.name: Reduction by symmetry
nodes.statement: By symmetry it is sufficient to establish the first equality in \eqref {asseq}.
nodes.statement_short: By symmetry prove only the first equality

nodes.name: First inequality
nodes.statement:
Observe that \eqref {rktinfrel} implies that $\rkts {Q, R, S} \geqslant \rkts {Q, R}$, and another application of Proposition~\ref {rktinf}
yields $\rkts {Q, R, S} \geqslant \rkts {\rkts {Q, R}, S}$.
nodes.statement_short: Minimality of the RK transform gives one inequality

nodes.name: Converse inequality
nodes.statement:
Let us verify the converse inequality.  Suppose that $w \in X_+$.  Then for any $x, y, z \in X_+$ such that $x + y + z \leqslant w$
we have
$$
\rkt {\rkts {Q, R}, S} {w} \geqslant \rkt {Q, R} {x + y} + S (z) \geqslant Q (x) + R (y) + S (z),
$$
so $\rkts {\rkts {Q, R}, S} \geqslant \rkts {Q, R, S}$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the nested transform from below via three-term decompositions

nodes.name: General associativity of the Riesz-Kantorovich transform
nodes.statement:
It is easy to see that the Riesz-Kantorovich transform of any finite number of maps
is stable under arbitrary association of terms in the spirit of Proposition~\ref {rkass}.
conclusions: the Riesz-Kantorovich transform of any finite number of maps is stable under arbitrary association of terms

nodes.name: Inequality in the RK transform cannot be replaced by equality
nodes.statement:
A moment's reflection shows that it is generally not the case.
For example, let $X = \mathbb R^3$ with the standard lattice order
$X_+ = \left\{ (x, y, z) \mid x, y, z \geqslant 0 \right\}$ that appeared in Section~\ref {lrdps} above,
and let $f ((x, y, z)) = -x + y - z$ and $g ((x, y, z)) = x - y - z$.
Contemplating the extreme points of the order interval $[0, (x, y, z)]$ relative to the gradients
$(-1, 1, -1)$ and $(1, -1, 1)$ of $f$ and $g$, one immediately notices that
the supremum in \eqref {rktdef} for $\rkt {f, g} {(x, y, z)}$, $(x, y, z) \in X_+$, is attained
at a decomposition $(0, y, 0) + (x, 0, 0)$, which is strictly smaller than $(x, y, z)$ in the order of $X$ unless $z = 0$,
and that the corresponding supremum value
$$
\rkt {f, g} {(x, y, z)} = x + y
$$
would not have been attained had we replaced
inequality in the definition \eqref {rktdef} by equality.
nodes.statement_short: For two functionals on $\mathbb R^3$ the supremum in the RK transform is attained only at a decomposition strictly below $x$.

nodes.name: RK transform with a positive map uses exact decompositions
nodes.statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be ordered linear spaces, $n \geqslant 1$ and let $T = \left\{T_1, \ldots, T_n\right\}$ be a finite collection of linear maps $T_j : X_+ \to Y$ for $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$. Suppose also that $T_l \geqslant 0$ for some $1 \leqslant l \leqslant n$. Then \begin{multline} \rkt {T} {x} = \sup \left\{ \sum_{j = 1}^n T_j (x_j) \mid x_j \in X_+ \text { for $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$ and } \sum_{j = 1}^n x_j = x \right\}. \end{multline}
also_stated_at:
However, it is easy to see that if one of the maps $T_j$ is positive then the supremum in \eqref {rktdef}
is attained at some decomposition $\sum_{j = 1}^n x_j = x$.
assumptions: $X$ and $Y$ be ordered linear spaces, $n \geqslant 1$
$T = \left\{T_1, \ldots, T_n\right\}$ be a finite collection of linear maps $T_j : X_+ \to Y$ for $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$
$T_l \geqslant 0$ for some $1 \leqslant l \leqslant n$
conclusions: \rkt {T} {x} = \sup \left\{ \sum_{j = 1}^n T_j (x_j) \mid x_j \in X_+ \text { for $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$ and } \sum_{j = 1}^n x_j = x \right\}.
nodes.label: rkteq

nodes.name: RK transform over exact decompositions
nodes.statement: \rkt {T} {x} = \sup \left\{ \sum_{j = 1}^n T_j (x_j) \mid x_j \in X_+ \text { for $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$ and } \sum_{j = 1}^n x_j = x \right\}.
nodes.label: rktdefeq

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 11
nodes.statement:
Indeed, the value of the right-hand part of \eqref {rktdefeq} is less or equal than $\rkt {T} {x}$ because the supremum is taken over a smaller
set of decompositions.
On the other hand, let $\sum_{j = 1}^n x_j \leqslant x$ be
any decomposition
in the definition \eqref {rktdef}.  Then we can construct another decomposition $x = \sum_{j = 1}^n \tilde x_j$ by taking
$\tilde x_j = x_j$ for $j \neq l$ and $\tilde x_l = x_l + \left[x - \sum_{j = 1}^n x_j\right]$ so that
 
$
\sum_{j = 1}^n T_j (\tilde x_j) = \sum_{j = 1}^n T_j (x_j) + T_l \left( x - \sum_{j = 1}^n x_j \right) \geqslant 
\sum_{j = 1}^n T_j (x_j).
$
It follows that 
\begin{multline*}
\rkt {T} {x} \leqslant
\sup \left\{ \sum_{j = 1}^n T_j (x_j) \mid x_j \in X_+ \text { for $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$ and } \sum_{j = 1}^n x_j = x \right\},
\end{multline*}
which establishes \eqref {rktdefeq}.
nodes.statement_short: Fewer decompositions give a smaller sup; conversely add the slack $x-\sum x_j$ to the positive map's component.

nodes.name: Easy inequality
nodes.statement:
Indeed, the value of the right-hand part of \eqref {rktdefeq} is less or equal than $\rkt {T} {x}$ because the supremum is taken over a smaller
set of decompositions.
nodes.statement_short: Exact decompositions give at most $\mathcal R(T)(x)$

nodes.name: Slack construction
nodes.statement:
On the other hand, let $\sum_{j = 1}^n x_j \leqslant x$ be
any decomposition
in the definition \eqref {rktdef}.  Then we can construct another decomposition $x = \sum_{j = 1}^n \tilde x_j$ by taking
$\tilde x_j = x_j$ for $j \neq l$ and $\tilde x_l = x_l + \left[x - \sum_{j = 1}^n x_j\right]$ so that
 
$
\sum_{j = 1}^n T_j (\tilde x_j) = \sum_{j = 1}^n T_j (x_j) + T_l \left( x - \sum_{j = 1}^n x_j \right) \geqslant 
\sum_{j = 1}^n T_j (x_j).
$
nodes.statement_short: Move the slack into the positive map's argument to get an exact decomposition with larger value

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement_short: Conclude the reverse inequality

nodes.name: Reduction to the positive transform of one map
nodes.statement:
Propositions~\ref {rkass} and \ref {rktdefeq} allow us to reduce many questions regarding the general Reisz-Kantorovich transform
to the case of $\rktps {T}$ of a single map $T$.

nodes.name: Argument for Proposition 12
nodes.statement:
Observe that \eqref {rktdefeq} implies that
$$
\rkts {Q, R} = \rkts {0, Q - R} + R = \rktps {Q - R} + R
$$
for a positive linear operator $R \geqslant 0$ and a superlinerar map $Q$. Combining this with Proposition~\ref {rkass}
leads to the following useful observation.
nodes.statement_short: Write $\mathcal R(Q,R) = \mathcal R^+(Q-R) + R$ for positive $R$ and combine with associativity.

nodes.name: Reduction to positive transforms of single operators
nodes.statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be ordered linear spaces and $\mathcal L \subset \linop {X} {Y}$ a linear space. Suppose that for any $T \in \mathcal L$ the Riesz-Kantorovich transform $\rktps {T}$ is well-defined and $\rktps {T} \in \mathcal L$. Then for any finite collection of operators $T = \{T_1, \ldots, T_n\}$, $T_j \in \mathcal L$, $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$, such that $T_l \geqslant 0$ for some $1 \leqslant l \leqslant n$, we also have $\rkts {T} = \rkts {T_1, \ldots, T_n} \in \mathcal L$.
assumptions: $X$ and $Y$ be ordered linear spaces and $\mathcal L \subset \linop {X} {Y}$ a linear space
for any $T \in \mathcal L$ the Riesz-Kantorovich transform $\rktps {T}$ is well-defined and $\rktps {T} \in \mathcal L$
conclusions: for any finite collection of operators $T = \{T_1, \ldots, T_n\}$, $T_j \in \mathcal L$, $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$, such that $T_l \geqslant 0$ for some $1 \leqslant l \leqslant n$, we also have $\rkts {T} = \rkts {T_1, \ldots, T_n} \in \mathcal L$
nodes.label: onlysing

nodes.name: Linear RK transform is the supremum
nodes.statement:
Since every linear map is superlinear, Proposition~\ref {rktinf} implies that if the Riesz-Kantorovich transform $\rkts {T}$ of a finite collection
of \emph {linear} operators is well-defined and linear then $\rkts {T} = \bigvee_{j = 1}^n T_j$ in \linop {X_+} {Y} as well as in
\suplinop {X_+} {Y}.
assumptions: the Riesz-Kantorovich transform $\rkts {T}$ of a finite collection of \emph {linear} operators is well-defined and linear
conclusions: $\rkts {T} = \bigvee_{j = 1}^n T_j$ in \linop {X_+} {Y} as well as in \suplinop {X_+} {Y}

nodes.name: Derivation of the Riesz-Kantorovich theorem
nodes.statement:
This leads to the Riesz-Kantorovich theorem mentioned in Section~\ref {anintroduction} as soon as one
notices that the Riesz Decomposition Property of $X$ implies linearity of $\rktps {T}$ for any $T \in \blinop {X} {Y}$.

nodes.name: L-RDP is essentially linearity of the RK transform
nodes.statement:
More generally, it is not difficult to see that the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property
introduced in Section~\ref {lrdps} above is, in many cases, essentially
equivalent to linearity of the Riesz-Kantorovich transform.

nodes.name: L-RDP implies RK transforms stay in L
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces, $Y$ is a Dedekind complete lattice, $\mathcal L$ is a linear subspace of $\linop {X} {Y}$, $\rlinop {X} {Y} \subset \mathcal L$ and $X$ has the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property. Then for any finite collection of operators $T = \{T_1, \ldots, T_n\}$ such that $T_j \in \mathcal L$ for all $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$ and $T_l \geqslant 0$ for some $1 \leqslant l \leqslant n$, we also have $\rkts {T} \in \mathcal L$.
assumptions: $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces
$Y$ is a Dedekind complete lattice
$\mathcal L$ is a linear subspace of $\linop {X} {Y}$
$\rlinop {X} {Y} \subset \mathcal L$
$X$ has the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property
conclusions: for any finite collection of operators $T = \{T_1, \ldots, T_n\}$ such that $T_j \in \mathcal L$ for all $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$ and $T_l \geqslant 0$ for some $1 \leqslant l \leqslant n$, we also have $\rkts {T} \in \mathcal L$
nodes.label: lrdptorkf

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 13
nodes.statement:
Indeed, by Proposition~\ref {onlysing} it is sufficient to establish that for any $T \in \mathcal L$ the positive Riesz-Kantorovich
transform $\rktps {T}$ is linear; since $\rktps {T} \geqslant 0$, that would imply $\rktps {T} \in \mathcal L$ by the assumptions.
Since $\rktps {T}$ is superlinear, we have
$\rktp {T} {x + y} \geqslant \rktp {T} {x} + \rktp {T} {y}$ for all $x, y \in X_+$.
Suppose that this inequality is strict for some $x, y \in X_+$.  Then
$y_0 = \rktp {T} {x + y} - \rktp {T} {x} + \rktp {T} {y} > 0$, and from the definition of the supremum
it follows that
there exists some $z \in [0, x + y]$ such that
\begin{equation} T z \geqslant \frac 1 2 y_0 + \rktp {T} {x} + \rktp {T} {y} \geqslant
\frac 1 2 y_0 + T u + T v
\end{equation}
for all $u \in [0, x]$ and $v \in [0, y]$.
But \eqref {tseplrdp} means that $T$ strictly separates $z \in [0, x + y]$ from $[0, x] + [0, y]$,
which contradicts the assumption that $X$ satisfies the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property.
This concludes the proof of Proposition~\ref {lrdptorkf}.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to linearity of $\mathcal R^+(T)$; a strict superadditivity gap yields a point strictly separated by $T$, contradicting L-RDP.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement:
Indeed, by Proposition~\ref {onlysing} it is sufficient to establish that for any $T \in \mathcal L$ the positive Riesz-Kantorovich
transform $\rktps {T}$ is linear; since $\rktps {T} \geqslant 0$, that would imply $\rktps {T} \in \mathcal L$ by the assumptions.
nodes.statement_short: By Proposition 12 it suffices to show $\mathcal R^+(T)$ is linear

nodes.name: Superadditivity
nodes.statement:
Since $\rktps {T}$ is superlinear, we have
$\rktp {T} {x + y} \geqslant \rktp {T} {x} + \rktp {T} {y}$ for all $x, y \in X_+$.
nodes.statement_short: Superlinearity gives one inequality

nodes.name: Strict gap
nodes.statement:
Suppose that this inequality is strict for some $x, y \in X_+$.  Then
$y_0 = \rktp {T} {x + y} - \rktp {T} {x} + \rktp {T} {y} > 0$, and from the definition of the supremum
it follows that
there exists some $z \in [0, x + y]$ such that
\begin{equation} T z \geqslant \frac 1 2 y_0 + \rktp {T} {x} + \rktp {T} {y} \geqslant
\frac 1 2 y_0 + T u + T v
\end{equation}
for all $u \in [0, x]$ and $v \in [0, y]$.
nodes.statement_short: A strict gap produces $z$ with $Tz$ above all $Tu+Tv$

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement:
But \eqref {tseplrdp} means that $T$ strictly separates $z \in [0, x + y]$ from $[0, x] + [0, y]$,
which contradicts the assumption that $X$ satisfies the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property.
This concludes the proof of Proposition~\ref {lrdptorkf}.
nodes.statement_short: $T$ strictly separates $z$, contradicting L-RDP

nodes.name: Strict separation inequality
nodes.statement: T z \geqslant \frac 1 2 y_0 + \rktp {T} {x} + \rktp {T} {y} \geqslant \frac 1 2 y_0 + T u + T v
nodes.label: tseplrdp

nodes.name: Linear positive RK transforms imply L-RDP
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces and $\mathcal L$ is a linear subspace of $\linop {X} {Y}$. Suppose also that for any $T \in \mathcal L$ map $\rktps {T}$ is well-defined and linear. Then $X$ satisfies the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property.
assumptions: $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces and $\mathcal L$ is a linear subspace of $\linop {X} {Y}$
for any $T \in \mathcal L$ map $\rktps {T}$ is well-defined and linear
conclusions: $X$ satisfies the $\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property
nodes.label: lrdp

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 14
nodes.statement:
Suppose that, on the contrary, $X$ does not satisfy the
$\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property.  This means that there exist
some $x, y \in X_+$, $z \in [0, x + y] \setminus \left( [0, x] + [0, y]\right)$
and $T \in \mathcal L$
such that
$T$ strictly separates $z$ from $[0, x] + [0, y]$.
By changing the sign of $T$ if necessary we may assume that
\begin{equation} T z > \sup \{T (u + v) \mid u \in [0, x], v \in [0, y]\}.
\end{equation}
Let $y_0 = T z - \sup \{T (u + v) \mid u \in [0, x], v \in [0, y]\} > 0$.
Then \eqref {tztuv} implies that
\begin{equation} T z \geqslant y_0 + T u + T v
\end{equation}
for all $u \in [0, x]$ and $v \in [0, y]$.
Taking supremums of the right-hand part of \eqref {tztuv2} one after the other yields
\begin{multline*}
T z \geqslant y_0 + \sup \{T u \mid u \in [0, x]\} +
\sup \{T v \mid v \in [0, y]\} =
\\
y_0 + \rktp {T} {x} + \rktp {T} {y},
\end{multline*}
which implies that
\begin{equation} \rktp {T} {x + y} \geqslant T z \geqslant y_0 + \rktp {T} {x} + \rktp {T} {y}.
\end{equation}
However, $\rktps {T}$ is linear by the assumptions, so
$$
\rktp {T} {x + y} = \rktp {T} {x} + \rktp {T} {y},
$$
which contradicts
\eqref {tztuv3} since $y_0 > 0$.  The proof of Proposition~\ref {lrdp} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: A strictly separating $T$ gives $\mathcal R^+(T)(x+y) > \mathcal R^+(T)(x)+\mathcal R^+(T)(y)$, contradicting linearity.

nodes.name: Contradiction hypothesis
nodes.statement:
Suppose that, on the contrary, $X$ does not satisfy the
$\mathcal L$-Riesz Decomposition Property.  This means that there exist
some $x, y \in X_+$, $z \in [0, x + y] \setminus \left( [0, x] + [0, y]\right)$
and $T \in \mathcal L$
such that
$T$ strictly separates $z$ from $[0, x] + [0, y]$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume L-RDP fails: some $T$ strictly separates a bad point $z$

nodes.name: Sign normalization
nodes.statement_short: Normalize the sign of $T$

nodes.name: Gap
nodes.statement:
Let $y_0 = T z - \sup \{T (u + v) \mid u \in [0, x], v \in [0, y]\} > 0$.
Then \eqref {tztuv} implies that
\begin{equation} T z \geqslant y_0 + T u + T v
\end{equation}
for all $u \in [0, x]$ and $v \in [0, y]$.
nodes.statement_short: Quantify the gap $y_0>0$

nodes.name: Supremum bound
nodes.statement_short: Take suprema to get $\mathcal R^+(T)(x+y) \ge y_0 + \mathcal R^+(T)(x) + \mathcal R^+(T)(y)$

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement:
However, $\rktps {T}$ is linear by the assumptions, so
$$
\rktp {T} {x + y} = \rktp {T} {x} + \rktp {T} {y},
$$
which contradicts
\eqref {tztuv3} since $y_0 > 0$.  The proof of Proposition~\ref {lrdp} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Linearity contradicts the gap

nodes.name: Strict separation of z
nodes.statement: T z > \sup \{T (u + v) \mid u \in [0, x], v \in [0, y]\}.
nodes.label: tztuv

nodes.name: Gap inequality
nodes.statement: T z \geqslant y_0 + T u + T v
nodes.label: tztuv2

nodes.name: Superadditivity gap for the positive transform
nodes.statement: \rktp {T} {x + y} \geqslant T z \geqslant y_0 + \rktp {T} {x} + \rktp {T} {y}.
nodes.label: tztuv3

nodes.name: Dominating lemma is essentially equivalent to the main results
nodes.statement:
It is not difficult to see that (at least under some additional assumptions)
the validity of this lemma for Riesz-Kantorovich transforms in place of superlinear maps $p$
is more or less equivalent to validity of the main results in
Section~\ref {rkf} below concerning lattice and decomposition properties of a space of linear operators between two ordered linear spaces.

nodes.name: Dominating operator at an internal point
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ is an ordered linear space such that $x \in X_+$ is an internal point of $X_+$ and $Y$ is a Dedekind complete lattice. Suppose also that $p : X_+ \to Y$ is a superlinear map and $y \in Y$ satisfies $y \geqslant p (x)$. Then there exists a linear operator $M : X \to Y$ such that $M \geqslant p$ and $M x = y$.
assumptions: $X$ is an ordered linear space such that $x \in X_+$ is an internal point of $X_+$
$Y$ is a Dedekind complete lattice
$p : X_+ \to Y$ is a superlinear map
$y \in Y$ satisfies $y \geqslant p (x)$
conclusions: there exists a linear operator $M : X \to Y$ such that $M \geqslant p$ and $M x = y$
nodes.label: suprtli

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 15
nodes.statement:
Indeed, observe that if $x$ is an internal point of $X_+$ (equivalently, an order unit of $X$)
then the space $L = \{\alpha x \mid \alpha \in \mathbb R\}$ spanned by
$x$ satisfies $X_+ + L = X$. 
Let $M_0 : \{\lambda x \mid \lambda > 0 \} \to Y$ be a map defined by $M_0 (\lambda x) = \lambda y$ for all $\lambda > 0$.
Then $M_0 \geqslant p$ on the domain of $M_0$.
We see that $M_0$ satisfies the conditions of the Hahn-Banach theorem (see Section~\ref {ovl}),
and thus $M_0$ can be extended to a linear map $M$ satisfying the conclusion of Lemma~\ref {suprtli}.
nodes.statement_short: Define $M_0$ on the ray through $x$ and extend it by the Hahn-Banach Theorem with superlinear minorant $p$.

nodes.name: Span of the order unit
nodes.statement:
Indeed, observe that if $x$ is an internal point of $X_+$ (equivalently, an order unit of $X$)
then the space $L = \{\alpha x \mid \alpha \in \mathbb R\}$ spanned by
$x$ satisfies $X_+ + L = X$.
nodes.statement_short: The line through the order unit $x$ satisfies $X_+ + L = X$

nodes.name: Initial map
nodes.statement:
Let $M_0 : \{\lambda x \mid \lambda > 0 \} \to Y$ be a map defined by $M_0 (\lambda x) = \lambda y$ for all $\lambda > 0$.
Then $M_0 \geqslant p$ on the domain of $M_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $M_0(\lambda x) = \lambda y$, which dominates $p$

nodes.name: Hahn-Banach extension
nodes.statement:
We see that $M_0$ satisfies the conditions of the Hahn-Banach theorem (see Section~\ref {ovl}),
and thus $M_0$ can be extended to a linear map $M$ satisfying the conclusion of Lemma~\ref {suprtli}.
nodes.statement_short: Extend by the Hahn-Banach Theorem

nodes.name: Continuous dominating functional
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ is an ordered linear space equipped with a locally convex topology (not necessarily Hausdorff) such that the cone $X_+$ is generating for $X$. Suppose also that $p : X_+ \to \mathbb R$ is a continuous superlinear map and points $x \in X_+$, $y \in \mathbb R$ satisfy $y > p (x)$. Then there exists a continous linear functional $M : X \to \mathbb R$ such that $M \geqslant p$ and $M (x) < y$.
assumptions: $X$ is an ordered linear space equipped with a locally convex topology (not necessarily Hausdorff) such that the cone $X_+$ is generating for $X$
$p : X_+ \to \mathbb R$ is a continuous superlinear map
points $x \in X_+$, $y \in \mathbb R$ satisfy $y > p (x)$
conclusions: there exists a continous linear functional $M : X \to \mathbb R$ such that $M \geqslant p$ and $M (x) < y$
nodes.label: suprtlf0

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 16
nodes.statement:
This lemma is a little more involved since we cannot in general just invoke the Hahn-Banach theorem in the absence of interior points;
however, with a bit of topological reasoning we can instead make use of a separation theorem.
Let
$\Gamma = \{ (z, t) \mid z \in X_+, t \leqslant p (x) \}$ be the subgraph of $p$, that is the epigraph of $-p$ turned upside down,
and let $G = \bar \Gamma$ be its closure in $X \times \mathbb R$.
Observe that since $p$ is continuous, $\Gamma$ is closed in $X_+ \times \mathbb R$ equipped with the relative topology induced by $X \times \mathbb R$.
Indeed, for every $z \in X_+$ and $t \neq p (z)$ there exists a neighbourhood $V \subset X_+$ of $z$ such that
$|p (a) - t| < \frac 1 2 |p (z) - t|$ for all $a \in V$; therefore $V \times (t - \frac 1 2 |p (z) - t|, t + \frac 1 2 |p (z) - t|)$
is an open neighbourhood of
$(z, t)$ that does not intersect the graph $\Gamma$.
Closedness of $\Gamma$ in $X_+ \times \mathbb R$ implies that $G \cap (X_+ \times \mathbb R) = \Gamma$:
inclusion $G \cap (X_+ \times \mathbb R) \supset \Gamma$ is trivial, and nonemptiness of
$\left[G \cap (X_+ \times \mathbb R)\right] \setminus \Gamma$ would contradict relative closedness of $\Gamma$ in $X_+ \times \mathbb R$
since every point of $G \cap (X_+ \times \mathbb R)$ belongs to the closure of $\Gamma$ in $X_+ \times \mathbb R$.
In particular, $(x, y) \notin G$ since $(x, y) \notin \Gamma$.
Therefore point
$(x, y)$ belongs to $(X \times \mathbb R) \setminus G$, which is an open set in the locally convex linear topological space $X \times \mathbb R$,
and so there exists a convex open neighbourhood $U \ni (x, y)$ that
does not intersect $G$.
Superlinearity of $p$ implies that $\Gamma$ is a convex cone,
and therefore $G$ is also a convex cone as a closure of a convex cone in the linear topological space $X \times \mathbb R$.
Let $W = \bigcup_{\lambda > 0} \lambda U$ be the conic hull of $U$. $W$ is open because $U$ is open.
Since $G$ is a cone and $U$ does not intersect $G$, it is easy to see
that $W$ also does not intersect $G$.
By the Hahn-Banach separation theorem there exists a linear functional $f : X \times \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ that separates $G$ and~$W$,
that is
$s = \sup \{f (b) \mid b \in G \} < f (c)$ for all $c \in W$.  Since $W$ is open and nonempty, $f$ is continuous.
Now it remains to verify that $D = \{(z, t) \mid f ((z, t)) = s\}$ is a graph of a functional $M$ that satisfies the conclusion of Lemma~\ref {suprtlf0}.
First, observe that $\{f ((z, t)) \mid t \in \mathbb R\} = \mathbb R$ for all $z \in X_+$:
since by linearity $f ((z, t)) = f ((x, t)) + f ((z - x, 0))$, it is sufficient to establish that
$f (x, \mathbb R) = \{f ((x, t)) \mid t \in \mathbb R\} = \mathbb R$,
and this follows easily from the fact that $f (x, \mathbb R)$ is a linear subspace of $\mathbb R$ that cannot be trivial since
$f ((x, p (x))) < f ((x, y))$.  So $D$ is indeed a graph of a functional
$M : X \to \mathbb R$, which is continuous since $f$ is continuous and therefore $D$ is closed.
Linearity of $f$ implies that $M$ is affine, and from the fact that $f$ separates two cones it follows that $f (0, 0) = s$
