and $M (0) = 0$, i.~e. $M$ is linear.  Since the epigraph of $M$ contains an open set $U$, the epigraph of $M$ has nonempty interior
and thus $M$ is continuous.
Finally, $M \geqslant p$ because $f ((z, p (z))) \leqslant s$ for all $z \in X_+$, and 
$M (x) < y$ because $f ((x, M (x))) = s < f ((x, y))$.  The proof of Lemma~\ref {suprtlf0} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Separate the closed subgraph cone of $p$ from the conic hull of a neighbourhood of $(x,y)$; the separating hyperplane is the graph of $M$. Key step: closedness of the subgraph from continuity of $p$.

nodes.name: Strategy
nodes.statement:
This lemma is a little more involved since we cannot in general just invoke the Hahn-Banach theorem in the absence of interior points;
however, with a bit of topological reasoning we can instead make use of a separation theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Use a separation theorem instead of Hahn-Banach extension

nodes.name: Subgraph and its closedness
nodes.statement:
Let
$\Gamma = \{ (z, t) \mid z \in X_+, t \leqslant p (x) \}$ be the subgraph of $p$, that is the epigraph of $-p$ turned upside down,
and let $G = \bar \Gamma$ be its closure in $X \times \mathbb R$.
Observe that since $p$ is continuous, $\Gamma$ is closed in $X_+ \times \mathbb R$ equipped with the relative topology induced by $X \times \mathbb R$.
Indeed, for every $z \in X_+$ and $t \neq p (z)$ there exists a neighbourhood $V \subset X_+$ of $z$ such that
$|p (a) - t| < \frac 1 2 |p (z) - t|$ for all $a \in V$; therefore $V \times (t - \frac 1 2 |p (z) - t|, t + \frac 1 2 |p (z) - t|)$
is an open neighbourhood of
$(z, t)$ that does not intersect the graph $\Gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the subgraph $\Gamma$ of $p$ and its closure $G$; continuity of $p$ makes $\Gamma$ relatively closed

nodes.name: Trace of the closure
nodes.statement:
Closedness of $\Gamma$ in $X_+ \times \mathbb R$ implies that $G \cap (X_+ \times \mathbb R) = \Gamma$:
inclusion $G \cap (X_+ \times \mathbb R) \supset \Gamma$ is trivial, and nonemptiness of
$\left[G \cap (X_+ \times \mathbb R)\right] \setminus \Gamma$ would contradict relative closedness of $\Gamma$ in $X_+ \times \mathbb R$
since every point of $G \cap (X_+ \times \mathbb R)$ belongs to the closure of $\Gamma$ in $X_+ \times \mathbb R$.
In particular, $(x, y) \notin G$ since $(x, y) \notin \Gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $G$ meets $X_+\times\mathbb R$ only in $\Gamma$, so $(x,y)\notin G$

nodes.name: Neighbourhood U
nodes.statement:
Therefore point
$(x, y)$ belongs to $(X \times \mathbb R) \setminus G$, which is an open set in the locally convex linear topological space $X \times \mathbb R$,
and so there exists a convex open neighbourhood $U \ni (x, y)$ that
does not intersect $G$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose a convex open neighbourhood $U$ of $(x,y)$ missing $G$

nodes.name: Convex cones
nodes.statement:
Superlinearity of $p$ implies that $\Gamma$ is a convex cone,
and therefore $G$ is also a convex cone as a closure of a convex cone in the linear topological space $X \times \mathbb R$.
nodes.statement_short: $\Gamma$ and $G$ are convex cones

nodes.name: Conic hull W
nodes.statement:
Let $W = \bigcup_{\lambda > 0} \lambda U$ be the conic hull of $U$. $W$ is open because $U$ is open.
Since $G$ is a cone and $U$ does not intersect $G$, it is easy to see
that $W$ also does not intersect $G$.
nodes.statement_short: The open conic hull $W$ of $U$ misses $G$

nodes.name: Separation
nodes.statement:
By the Hahn-Banach separation theorem there exists a linear functional $f : X \times \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ that separates $G$ and~$W$,
that is
$s = \sup \{f (b) \mid b \in G \} < f (c)$ for all $c \in W$.  Since $W$ is open and nonempty, $f$ is continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Separate $G$ and $W$ by a continuous functional $f$

nodes.name: Remaining claim
nodes.statement: Now it remains to verify that $D = \{(z, t) \mid f ((z, t)) = s\}$ is a graph of a functional $M$ that satisfies the conclusion of Lemma~\ref {suprtlf0}.
nodes.statement_short: It remains to show the level set $D$ is the graph of the required $M$

nodes.name: D is a graph
nodes.statement:
First, observe that $\{f ((z, t)) \mid t \in \mathbb R\} = \mathbb R$ for all $z \in X_+$:
since by linearity $f ((z, t)) = f ((x, t)) + f ((z - x, 0))$, it is sufficient to establish that
$f (x, \mathbb R) = \{f ((x, t)) \mid t \in \mathbb R\} = \mathbb R$,
and this follows easily from the fact that $f (x, \mathbb R)$ is a linear subspace of $\mathbb R$ that cannot be trivial since
$f ((x, p (x))) < f ((x, y))$.  So $D$ is indeed a graph of a functional
$M : X \to \mathbb R$, which is continuous since $f$ is continuous and therefore $D$ is closed.
nodes.statement_short: $D$ is the graph of a continuous functional $M$

nodes.name: Linearity of M
nodes.statement:
Linearity of $f$ implies that $M$ is affine, and from the fact that $f$ separates two cones it follows that $f (0, 0) = s$
and $M (0) = 0$, i.~e. $M$ is linear.  Since the epigraph of $M$ contains an open set $U$, the epigraph of $M$ has nonempty interior
and thus $M$ is continuous.
nodes.statement_short: $M$ is linear and continuous

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement:
Finally, $M \geqslant p$ because $f ((z, p (z))) \leqslant s$ for all $z \in X_+$, and 
$M (x) < y$ because $f ((x, M (x))) = s < f ((x, y))$.  The proof of Lemma~\ref {suprtlf0} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Verify $M \ge p$ and $M(x) < y$

nodes.name: Continuity of the Riesz-Kantorovich transform
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ is an ordered linear topological space. Then for any continuous linear functionals $T = \{T_1, \ldots, T_n\}$, where $T_j : X \to \mathbb R$, $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$, the Riesz-Kantorovich transform $\rkts {T}$, assuming it is well-defined, is also continuous.
assumptions: $X$ is an ordered linear topological space
continuous linear functionals $T = \{T_1, \ldots, T_n\}$, where $T_j : X \to \mathbb R$, $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$
assuming it is well-defined
conclusions: the Riesz-Kantorovich transform $\rkts {T}$, assuming it is well-defined, is also continuous
nodes.label: rktc

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 17
nodes.statement:
Indeed, suppose that $\rkt {T} {x} = y$ for some $x \in X_+$ and $y \in \mathbb R$ and we are given an open neighbourhood
$(y - \varepsilon, y + \varepsilon) \subset U \subset \mathbb R$ of $y$, $\varepsilon > 0$;
we need to find an open neighbourhood $V \subset X_+$ of $x$ satisfying $\rkt {T} {V} \subset U$.
Let $W = \left(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon\right) \subset \mathbb R$, so that $y + W \subset U$.
Observe that a map $S : X^n \to \mathbb R$ defined by $S ((x_1, \ldots, x_n)) = \sum_{j = 1}^n T_j (x_j)$ is linear and continuous in $x_j \in X$,
$1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$, as a composition of continuous maps.
Moreover, $S$ is uniformly continuous because of its linearity, i.~e. there exists an open neighbourhood
$V_1$ of $0$ such that
\begin{equation} S ((x_1 + V_1, \ldots, x_n + V_1)) \subset S ((x_1, \ldots, x_n)) + W
\end{equation}
for all $x_j \in X$, $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$.
Now let $V \subset X$ be an open balanced (i.~e. $V = -V$) neighbourhood of $0$ satisfying $V \subset V_1$.
Inclusion \eqref {unicont} implies that
\begin{equation} \rkt {T} {z_1} \geqslant \rkt {T} {z_0} - \varepsilon
\end{equation}
for all $z_0 \in X_+$ and $z_1 \in \left( z_0 + \sum_{k = 1}^n V \right) \cap X_+$.
By setting $z_0 = x$ and $z_1 = x$ separately in \eqref {tzx} we arrive at the required continuity relation
$|\rkt {T} {z} - \rkt {T} {x}| \leqslant \varepsilon$ for all $z \in x + \sum_{k = 1}^n V$.  The proof of Proposition~\ref {rktc} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Uniform continuity of the linear map $(x_j) \mapsto \sum T_j(x_j)$ gives a two-sided $\varepsilon$ bound on the RK transform.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement_short: State what is needed for continuity at $x$

nodes.name: Map S
nodes.statement:
Let $W = \left(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon\right) \subset \mathbb R$, so that $y + W \subset U$.
Observe that a map $S : X^n \to \mathbb R$ defined by $S ((x_1, \ldots, x_n)) = \sum_{j = 1}^n T_j (x_j)$ is linear and continuous in $x_j \in X$,
$1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$, as a composition of continuous maps.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $W$ and the continuous linear map $S$

nodes.name: Uniform continuity
nodes.statement:
Moreover, $S$ is uniformly continuous because of its linearity, i.~e. there exists an open neighbourhood
$V_1$ of $0$ such that
\begin{equation} S ((x_1 + V_1, \ldots, x_n + V_1)) \subset S ((x_1, \ldots, x_n)) + W
\end{equation}
for all $x_j \in X$, $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$.
nodes.statement_short: Uniform continuity of $S$

nodes.name: One-sided bound
nodes.statement:
Now let $V \subset X$ be an open balanced (i.~e. $V = -V$) neighbourhood of $0$ satisfying $V \subset V_1$.
Inclusion \eqref {unicont} implies that
\begin{equation} \rkt {T} {z_1} \geqslant \rkt {T} {z_0} - \varepsilon
\end{equation}
for all $z_0 \in X_+$ and $z_1 \in \left( z_0 + \sum_{k = 1}^n V \right) \cap X_+$.
nodes.statement_short: Deduce the one-sided bound (tzx)

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement:
By setting $z_0 = x$ and $z_1 = x$ separately in \eqref {tzx} we arrive at the required continuity relation
$|\rkt {T} {z} - \rkt {T} {x}| \leqslant \varepsilon$ for all $z \in x + \sum_{k = 1}^n V$.  The proof of Proposition~\ref {rktc} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Apply it both ways to conclude

nodes.name: Uniform continuity of S
nodes.statement: S ((x_1 + V_1, \ldots, x_n + V_1)) \subset S ((x_1, \ldots, x_n)) + W
nodes.label: unicont

nodes.name: Lower semicontinuity estimate
nodes.statement: \rkt {T} {z_1} \geqslant \rkt {T} {z_0} - \varepsilon
nodes.label: tzx

nodes.name: Archimedean ordered space
nodes.statement:
Recall that an ordered linear space $Y$ is called \emph {Archimedean} if for any $y \in Y$ and $x \in Y_+$ inequalities $n y \leqslant x$ for all
$n \geqslant 1$ imply that $y \leqslant 0$.

nodes.name: Interior cone defines the same operator order
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces and $\mathrm{int} X_+ \neq 0$. Suppose also that $Y$ is an Archimedean Dedekind complete lattice. Then $X$ ordered by $\{0\} \cup \mathrm{int} X_+$ defines the same order in $\linop {X} {Y}$ as does $X$ ordered by $X_+$.
assumptions: $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces and $\mathrm{int} X_+ \neq 0$
$Y$ is an Archimedean Dedekind complete lattice
conclusions: $X$ ordered by $\{0\} \cup \mathrm{int} X_+$ defines the same order in $\linop {X} {Y}$ as does $X$ ordered by $X_+$
nodes.label: isameorder

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 18
nodes.statement:
Indeed, suppose that $T \in \linop {X} {Y}$ and $T x \geqslant 0$ for all $x \in \mathrm{int} X_+$ under the assumptions of Proposition~\ref {isameorder};
we need to verify that $T x \geqslant 0$ for all $x \in X_+$.  Fix any $x_0 \in \mathrm{int} X_+$ and let
$x_\theta = (1 - \theta) x_0 + \theta x$ for $0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 1$.
Since $x_\theta \in \mathrm{int} X_+$ for $0 \leqslant \theta < 1$, by the assumptions
$T (x_\theta) \geqslant 0$ for $0 \leqslant \theta < 1$, and it suffices to verify that $T (x_1) \geqslant 0$.
Since $Y$ is a Dedekind complete lattice, there exists
$y_\alpha = \inf \{T (x_\theta) \mid \alpha \leqslant \theta < 1\}$ for all $0 \leqslant \alpha < 1$ and $y_\alpha \geqslant 0$.
Linearity of $T (x_\theta)$ in $\theta$ implies that
$$
T (x_\alpha) \wedge T (x_1) \leqslant T (x_\theta) \leqslant T (x_\alpha) \vee T (x_1)
$$
for all
$\alpha \leqslant \theta \leqslant 1$,
so 
\begin{equation} 0 \vee [T (x_\alpha) \wedge T (x_1)] \leqslant y_\alpha \leqslant T (x_\alpha) \vee T (x_1)
\end{equation}
for all $0 < \alpha < 1$.
Now observe that linearity of $T (x_\theta)$ in $\theta$ also implies that the set-valued map
$\alpha \mapsto \{y \in Y \mid y \geqslant T (x_\alpha), y \geqslant T (x_1)\}$ is affine in $0 \leqslant \alpha \leqslant 1$,
so $\alpha \mapsto T (x_\alpha) \vee T (x_1)$ and likewise $\alpha \mapsto T (x_\alpha) \wedge T (x_1)$ are affine in $0 \leqslant \alpha \leqslant 1$;
therefore $\varphi (\alpha) = T (x_\alpha) \vee T (x_1) - T (x_\alpha) \wedge T (x_1)$ is an affine positive map and $\varphi (1) = 0$.
In particular,
$$
T (x_\alpha) \vee T (x_1) = T (x_\alpha) \wedge T (x_1) + \varphi (\alpha) \leqslant T (x_1) + \varphi (0),
$$
so
the set of values of the right-hand part of \eqref {veeest} has an upper bound.
Let
$$
m_1 = \sup \{T (x_\alpha) \wedge T (x_1) \mid 0 \leqslant \alpha < 1\},
$$
$$
y_1 = \sup \{y_\alpha \mid 0 \leqslant \alpha < 1\}
$$
and
$$
M_1 = \inf \{T (x_\alpha) \vee T (x_1) \mid 0 \leqslant \alpha < 1\}.
$$
It is easy to see that $0 \leqslant m_1 \leqslant y_1 \leqslant M_1$;
moreover,
$$
M_1 - m_1 \leqslant \varphi (\alpha) = (1 - \alpha) \varphi (0)
$$
for all $0 \leqslant \alpha < 1$, so
the Archimedean property of $Y$ implies that $M_1 - m_1 \leqslant 0$, and thus $0 \leqslant m_1 = y_1 = M_1$.
Furthermore,
$$
m_1 \leqslant T (x_1) \leqslant M_1,
$$
which implies that $m_1 = M_1 = T (x_1)$, and therefore
$y_1 = T (x_1) \geqslant 0$.  The proof of Proposition~\ref {isameorder} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Approach $x$ along a segment from an internal point; affine squeezing of lattice bounds and the Archimedean property force $T(x) \ge 0$.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement:
Indeed, suppose that $T \in \linop {X} {Y}$ and $T x \geqslant 0$ for all $x \in \mathrm{int} X_+$ under the assumptions of Proposition~\ref {isameorder};
we need to verify that $T x \geqslant 0$ for all $x \in X_+$.
nodes.statement_short: Goal: positivity on $\mathrm{int} X_+$ implies positivity on $X_+$

nodes.name: Segment
nodes.statement:
Fix any $x_0 \in \mathrm{int} X_+$ and let
$x_\theta = (1 - \theta) x_0 + \theta x$ for $0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 1$.
Since $x_\theta \in \mathrm{int} X_+$ for $0 \leqslant \theta < 1$, by the assumptions
$T (x_\theta) \geqslant 0$ for $0 \leqslant \theta < 1$, and it suffices to verify that $T (x_1) \geqslant 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Segment $x_\theta$ from an internal point to $x$

nodes.name: Infima
nodes.statement:
Since $Y$ is a Dedekind complete lattice, there exists
$y_\alpha = \inf \{T (x_\theta) \mid \alpha \leqslant \theta < 1\}$ for all $0 \leqslant \alpha < 1$ and $y_\alpha \geqslant 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Define the infima $y_\alpha \ge 0$

nodes.name: Sandwich (veeest)
nodes.statement:
Linearity of $T (x_\theta)$ in $\theta$ implies that
$$
T (x_\alpha) \wedge T (x_1) \leqslant T (x_\theta) \leqslant T (x_\alpha) \vee T (x_1)
$$
for all
$\alpha \leqslant \theta \leqslant 1$,
so 
\begin{equation} 0 \vee [T (x_\alpha) \wedge T (x_1)] \leqslant y_\alpha \leqslant T (x_\alpha) \vee T (x_1)
\end{equation}
for all $0 < \alpha < 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Sandwich $y_\alpha$ between lattice combinations

nodes.name: Affine width
nodes.statement:
Now observe that linearity of $T (x_\theta)$ in $\theta$ also implies that the set-valued map
$\alpha \mapsto \{y \in Y \mid y \geqslant T (x_\alpha), y \geqslant T (x_1)\}$ is affine in $0 \leqslant \alpha \leqslant 1$,
so $\alpha \mapsto T (x_\alpha) \vee T (x_1)$ and likewise $\alpha \mapsto T (x_\alpha) \wedge T (x_1)$ are affine in $0 \leqslant \alpha \leqslant 1$;
therefore $\varphi (\alpha) = T (x_\alpha) \vee T (x_1) - T (x_\alpha) \wedge T (x_1)$ is an affine positive map and $\varphi (1) = 0$.
In particular,
$$
T (x_\alpha) \vee T (x_1) = T (x_\alpha) \wedge T (x_1) + \varphi (\alpha) \leqslant T (x_1) + \varphi (0),
$$
so
the set of values of the right-hand part of \eqref {veeest} has an upper bound.
nodes.statement_short: The width $\varphi$ is affine, vanishing at 1, giving an upper bound

nodes.name: Archimedean squeeze
nodes.statement:
Let
$$
m_1 = \sup \{T (x_\alpha) \wedge T (x_1) \mid 0 \leqslant \alpha < 1\},
$$
$$
y_1 = \sup \{y_\alpha \mid 0 \leqslant \alpha < 1\}
$$
and
$$
M_1 = \inf \{T (x_\alpha) \vee T (x_1) \mid 0 \leqslant \alpha < 1\}.
$$
It is easy to see that $0 \leqslant m_1 \leqslant y_1 \leqslant M_1$;
moreover,
$$
M_1 - m_1 \leqslant \varphi (\alpha) = (1 - \alpha) \varphi (0)
$$
for all $0 \leqslant \alpha < 1$, so
the Archimedean property of $Y$ implies that $M_1 - m_1 \leqslant 0$, and thus $0 \leqslant m_1 = y_1 = M_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Archimedean property collapses $m_1 \le y_1 \le M_1$

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement:
Furthermore,
$$
m_1 \leqslant T (x_1) \leqslant M_1,
$$
which implies that $m_1 = M_1 = T (x_1)$, and therefore
$y_1 = T (x_1) \geqslant 0$.  The proof of Proposition~\ref {isameorder} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $T(x_1) = y_1 \ge 0$

nodes.name: Bounds on y_alpha
nodes.statement: 0 \vee [T (x_\alpha) \wedge T (x_1)] \leqslant y_\alpha \leqslant T (x_\alpha) \vee T (x_1)
nodes.label: veeest

nodes.name: Dedekind completeness is needed in Proposition 18
nodes.statement:
We mention that Poposition~\ref {isameorder} may fail without the assumption that $Y$ is Dedekind complete;
it is easy to construct a finite-dimensional example with some closed $X_+$ and open $Y_+$.

nodes.name: Necessity of the Archimedean assumption
nodes.statement:
It is, however, not clear whether the assumption
that $Y$ is Archimedean is necessary for the conclusion of Proposition~\ref {isameorder}.

nodes.name: Riesz-Kantorovich formula for continuous functionals
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ is an ordered locally convex linear topological space, the cone $X_+$ is generating for $X$ and $\clinop {X} {\mathbb R} \subset \blinop {X} {\mathbb R}$. Then for any $T = \{T_1, \ldots, T_n\} \subset \clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ such that $\sup T$ exists in $\mathcal L = \clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ we have $\sup T = \rkts {T}$.
assumptions: $X$ is an ordered locally convex linear topological space
the cone $X_+$ is generating for $X$
$\clinop {X} {\mathbb R} \subset \blinop {X} {\mathbb R}$
$T = \{T_1, \ldots, T_n\} \subset \clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ such that $\sup T$ exists in $\mathcal L = \clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$
conclusions: $\sup T = \rkts {T}$
nodes.statement_short: If a finite set of continuous functionals has a supremum among continuous functionals, it equals the RK transform.
nodes.label: suprtc

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 19
nodes.statement:
Suppose that under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref {suprt}
$T \subset \clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$
is a finite collection of functionals such that the supremum of $T$ exists in $\clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$.
Let us denote this supremum by $S = \sup T$; we need to verify that $S = \rkts {T}$.
Observe that from Proposition~\ref {rktinf} it follows that $\rkts {T} \leqslant S$.
Now suppose that $\rkts {T} = S$ does not hold true, which means that there exists some $x \in X_+$
such that $\rkt {T} {x} < S (x)$.
 
 
By Proposition~\ref {rktc} the Riesz-Kantorovich trasform $\rkts {T}$ is continuous, and since it is superlinear
we can apply Lemma~\ref {suprtlf0} to points $x$ and $y = S (x)$ with $p = \rkts {T}$ to obtain a linear continuous functional $M \geqslant \rkts {T}$
satisfying $M (x) < S (x)$.
However, $S = \sup T$ implies that $S \leqslant M$ since $M \geqslant \rkts {T} \geqslant T_j$ for all $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$, and therefore
$M (x) \geqslant \sup T (x) = S (x)$.  This contradiction concludes the proof of Theorem~\ref {suprtc}.
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction: if $\mathcal R(T)(x) < S(x)$, Lemma 16 gives a continuous majorant $M$ of $\mathcal R(T)$ with $M(x) < S(x)$, violating $S = \sup T$.

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement:
Suppose that under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref {suprt}
$T \subset \clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$
is a finite collection of functionals such that the supremum of $T$ exists in $\clinop {X} {\mathbb R}$.
Let us denote this supremum by $S = \sup T$; we need to verify that $S = \rkts {T}$.
nodes.statement_short: Let $S = \sup T$; show $S = \mathcal R(T)$

nodes.name: Easy inequality
nodes.statement: Observe that from Proposition~\ref {rktinf} it follows that $\rkts {T} \leqslant S$.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 9 gives $\mathcal R(T) \le S$

nodes.name: Contradiction hypothesis
nodes.statement:
Now suppose that $\rkts {T} = S$ does not hold true, which means that there exists some $x \in X_+$
such that $\rkt {T} {x} < S (x)$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume strict inequality at some $x$

nodes.name: Dominating functional
nodes.statement:
By Proposition~\ref {rktc} the Riesz-Kantorovich trasform $\rkts {T}$ is continuous, and since it is superlinear
we can apply Lemma~\ref {suprtlf0} to points $x$ and $y = S (x)$ with $p = \rkts {T}$ to obtain a linear continuous functional $M \geqslant \rkts {T}$
satisfying $M (x) < S (x)$.
nodes.statement_short: Continuity (Prop. 17) and Lemma 16 give a continuous majorant $M$ with $M(x) < S(x)$

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement:
However, $S = \sup T$ implies that $S \leqslant M$ since $M \geqslant \rkts {T} \geqslant T_j$ for all $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$, and therefore
$M (x) \geqslant \sup T (x) = S (x)$.  This contradiction concludes the proof of Theorem~\ref {suprtc}.
nodes.statement_short: $M$ is an upper bound of $T$, so $M \ge S$: contradiction

nodes.name: Riesz-Kantorovich formula for order bounded functionals
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ is an ordered linear topological space, the cone $X_+$ is generating for $X$, and $\mathcal L$ is a linear space of linear functionals satisfying $\rlinop {X} {\mathbb R} \subset \mathcal L \subset \blinop {X} {\mathbb R}$. Then for any finite collection $T = \{T_1, \ldots, T_n\} \subset \mathcal L$ such that $\sup T$ exists in $\mathcal L$ we have $\sup T = \rkts {T}$.
assumptions: $X$ is an ordered linear topological space
the cone $X_+$ is generating for $X$
$\mathcal L$ is a linear space of linear functionals satisfying $\rlinop {X} {\mathbb R} \subset \mathcal L \subset \blinop {X} {\mathbb R}$
finite collection $T = \{T_1, \ldots, T_n\} \subset \mathcal L$ such that $\sup T$ exists in $\mathcal L$
conclusions: $\sup T = \rkts {T}$
nodes.statement_short: For functional spaces between regular and order bounded ones, an existing supremum of finitely many functionals equals the RK transform.
nodes.label: suprtf

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 20
nodes.statement:
Indeed, observe that the supremum $S = \sup T$ in $\mathcal L$ is also a supremum of $T$ in $\blinop {X} {\mathbb R}$,
since any upper bound $U \in \blinop {X} {\mathbb R}$ of $T$ also belongs to $\mathcal L$ because
$U \geqslant T_1$, so $U - T_1 \geqslant 0$ and $U$ is a sum of $T_1 \in \mathcal L$ and a regular operator $U - T_1$.
Equipping $X$ with its order topology (see Section~\ref {ovl}) reduces
Theorem~\ref {suprtf} at once to a
direct application of Theorem~\ref {suprtc}.
nodes.statement_short: The supremum in $\mathcal L$ is also one in the order bounded dual; with the order topology, Theorem 19 applies.

nodes.name: Riesz-Kantorovich formula on internal points
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces, the cone $X_+$ is generating for $X$, $X_+$ has an internal point, $Y$ is a Dedekind complete lattice and $\mathcal L \subset \linop {X} {Y}$ is a linear space of linear operators acting from $X$ to $Y$ satisfying $ \rlinop {X} {Y} \subset \mathcal L \subset \blinop {X} {Y}. $ Then for any $T = \{T_1, \ldots, T_n\} \subset \mathcal L$ such that $\sup T$ exists in $\mathcal L$ we have $\sup T (x) = \rkt {T} {x}$ for all $x \in \mathrm{int} X_+$.
assumptions: $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces
the cone $X_+$ is generating for $X$
$X_+$ has an internal point
$Y$ is a Dedekind complete lattice
$\mathcal L \subset \linop {X} {Y}$ is a linear space of linear operators acting from $X$ to $Y$ satisfying $ \rlinop {X} {Y} \subset \mathcal L \subset \blinop {X} {Y}. $
$T = \{T_1, \ldots, T_n\} \subset \mathcal L$ such that $\sup T$ exists in $\mathcal L$
conclusions: $\sup T (x) = \rkt {T} {x}$ for all $x \in \mathrm{int} X_+$
nodes.statement_short: If the cone has an internal point, an existing supremum of finitely many operators agrees with the RK transform on internal points.
nodes.label: suprt

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 21
nodes.statement:
The proof essentially repeats the proof of Theorem~\ref {suprtc} above with only a couple of small twists.
Suppose that 
$T \subset \mathcal L$ is a finite collection of operators under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref {suprt}
such that the supremum of $T$ exists in $\mathcal L$.
 
 
We denote this supremum by $S = \sup T$ and it is set upon us to verify that $S = \rkts {T}$ on the set of all internal points of $X_+$.
From Proposition~\ref {rktinf} it follows that $\rkts {T} \leqslant S$.
Suppose that $\rkt {T} {x} = S (x)$ does not hold true for all $x \in \mathrm{int} X_+$.
Then there exists some $x \in \mathrm{int} X_+$
such that $\rkt {T} {x} < S (x)$.
Let $y = \frac 1 2 \left( \rkt {T} {x} + S (x) \right)$; then
$\rkt {T} {x} < y < S (x)$.
By 
Lemma~\ref {suprtli}
there exists
a linear map $M \in \linop {X} {Y}$ such that
$M \geqslant \rkts {T}$ and $M (x) = y < S (x)$.  Observe that $M \geqslant T_1$, so $M - T_1 \in \rlinop {X} {Y}$ and therefore
 
$M \in \rlinop {X} {Y} + \mathcal L = \mathcal L$.
However, $S = \sup T$ in $\mathcal L$ implies that $S \leqslant M$, so
$M (x) \geqslant S (x)$.  This contradiction concludes the proof of Theorem~\ref {suprt}.
nodes.statement_short: As for Theorem 19, but Lemma 15 supplies a linear majorant $M$ of $\mathcal R(T)$ with $M(x) < S(x)$ at an internal point.

nodes.name: Strategy
nodes.statement: The proof essentially repeats the proof of Theorem~\ref {suprtc} above with only a couple of small twists.
nodes.statement_short: Same scheme as the proof of Theorem 19

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement:
Suppose that 
$T \subset \mathcal L$ is a finite collection of operators under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref {suprt}
such that the supremum of $T$ exists in $\mathcal L$.
 
 
We denote this supremum by $S = \sup T$ and it is set upon us to verify that $S = \rkts {T}$ on the set of all internal points of $X_+$.
nodes.statement_short: Let $S = \sup T$ in $\mathcal L$

nodes.name: Easy inequality
nodes.statement: From Proposition~\ref {rktinf} it follows that $\rkts {T} \leqslant S$.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 9 gives $\mathcal R(T) \le S$

nodes.name: Contradiction hypothesis
nodes.statement:
Suppose that $\rkt {T} {x} = S (x)$ does not hold true for all $x \in \mathrm{int} X_+$.
Then there exists some $x \in \mathrm{int} X_+$
such that $\rkt {T} {x} < S (x)$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume strict inequality at an internal point $x$

nodes.name: Dominating operator
nodes.statement:
Let $y = \frac 1 2 \left( \rkt {T} {x} + S (x) \right)$; then
$\rkt {T} {x} < y < S (x)$.
By 
Lemma~\ref {suprtli}
there exists
a linear map $M \in \linop {X} {Y}$ such that
$M \geqslant \rkts {T}$ and $M (x) = y < S (x)$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 15 gives a linear majorant $M$ with $M(x) = y < S(x)$

nodes.name: M lies in L
nodes.statement:
Observe that $M \geqslant T_1$, so $M - T_1 \in \rlinop {X} {Y}$ and therefore
 
$M \in \rlinop {X} {Y} + \mathcal L = \mathcal L$.
nodes.statement_short: $M - T_1$ is positive, so $M \in \mathcal L$

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement:
However, $S = \sup T$ in $\mathcal L$ implies that $S \leqslant M$, so
$M (x) \geqslant S (x)$.  This contradiction concludes the proof of Theorem~\ref {suprt}.
nodes.statement_short: $M \ge S$ contradicts $M(x) < S(x)$

nodes.name: Linearity of the RK transform on the whole cone
nodes.statement: Unfortunately, it does not seem to be clear whether $\rkts {T}$ is linear on all $X_+$ under the conditions of Theorem~\ref {suprt}.

nodes.name: Values on internal points determine operators
nodes.statement:
Luckily, however, this omission in our understanding of the Riesz-Kantorovich transform does not get in the way of the applications
connecting the properties of $X$ and $\mathcal L$, since the operators in $\mathcal L$ are uniquely defined by their values on $\mathrm{int} X_+$.

nodes.name: RDP of L suffices in the three cases
nodes.statement:
Let us now observe that in the same three cases treated in Theorems~\ref {suprtc}--\ref {suprt}
above we can replace the assumption that
$\sup S$ exists in $\mathcal L$ by the assumption that $\mathcal L$ has the Riesz Decomposition Property
and still arrive at the corresponding linearity of $\rkts {T}$.
assumptions: in the same three cases treated in Theorems~\ref {suprtc}--\ref {suprt}
$\mathcal L$ has the Riesz Decomposition Property
conclusions: the corresponding linearity of $\rkts {T}$

nodes.name: RDP of a functional space gives RK transforms in it
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ is an ordered linear space, the cone $X_+$ is generating for $X$, and $\mathcal L \subset \linop {X} {\mathbb R}$ is a linear space of linear functionals on $X$ satisfying $ \rlinop {X} {\mathbb R} \subset \mathcal L \subset \blinop {X} {\mathbb R}. $ Suppose also that $\mathcal L$ has the Riesz Decomposition Property. Then $\rkts {T} \in \mathcal L$ for any $T = \{T_1, \ldots, T_n\} \subset \mathcal L$.
assumptions: $X$ is an ordered linear space, the cone $X_+$ is generating for $X$
$\mathcal L \subset \linop {X} {\mathbb R}$ is a linear space of linear functionals on $X$ satisfying $ \rlinop {X} {\mathbb R} \subset \mathcal L \subset \blinop {X} {\mathbb R}. $
$\mathcal L$ has the Riesz Decomposition Property
conclusions: $\rkts {T} \in \mathcal L$ for any $T = \{T_1, \ldots, T_n\} \subset \mathcal L$
nodes.label: suprtrdpf

nodes.name: RDP of an operator space gives linear RK transforms on internal points
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces, the cone $X_+$ is generating for $X$, $X_+$ has an internal point, $Y$ is a Dedekind complete lattice and $\mathcal L \subset \linop {X} {Y}$ is a linear space of linear operators acting from $X$ to $Y$ satisfying $ \rlinop {X} {Y} \subset \mathcal L \subset \blinop {X} {Y}. $ Suppose also that $\mathcal L$ has the Riesz Decomposition Property. Then $\rkts {T}$ is linear on $\mathrm{int} X_+$ for any $T = \{T_1, \ldots, T_n\} \subset \mathcal L$, and the unique extension of $\rkts {T}$ restricted to $\mathrm{int} X_+$ to a linear operator from $\linop {X} {Y}$ belongs to~$\mathcal L$.
assumptions: $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces, the cone $X_+$ is generating for $X$
$X_+$ has an internal point, $Y$ is a Dedekind complete lattice
$\mathcal L \subset \linop {X} {Y}$ is a linear space of linear operators acting from $X$ to $Y$ satisfying $ \rlinop {X} {Y} \subset \mathcal L \subset \blinop {X} {Y}. $
$\mathcal L$ has the Riesz Decomposition Property
conclusions: $\rkts {T}$ is linear on $\mathrm{int} X_+$ for any $T = \{T_1, \ldots, T_n\} \subset \mathcal L$
the unique extension of $\rkts {T}$ restricted to $\mathrm{int} X_+$ to a linear operator from $\linop {X} {Y}$ belongs to~$\mathcal L$
nodes.label: suprtrdp

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 23
nodes.statement:
We will now give a proof for Proposition~\ref {suprtrdp} that also works as a proof of Proposition~\ref {suprtrdpf} with suitable apparent
minor modifications.
Indeed, under the assumptions of Proposition~\ref {suprtrdp} the Riesz-Kantorovich transform $\rkts {T}$ is well-defined and superlinear.
Suppose that it is not linear on $\mathrm{int} X_+$; this means that
$\rkt {T} {x + y} > \rkt {T} {x} + \rkt {T} {y}$

\end{equation}
By the same reasoning as in the proof of Theorem~\ref {suprt} we have $S_0, S_1 \in \mathcal L$.
Since by the assumption $\mathcal L$ has the Riesz Decomposition Property, it also has the interpolation property (see Section~\ref {ovl}).
Observe that $\{S_0, S_1\} \geqslant \rkts {T} \geqslant T$, so $\{S_0, S_1\} \geqslant T$, and by the interpolation property of $\mathcal L$

It follows that

\\

\end{multline}
so $S$ cannot be linear.  This contradiction concludes the proof of Proposition~\ref {suprtrdp}.

nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are ordered linear spaces, $X_+$ is a generating cone in $X$, $Y$ is a Dedekind complete lattice and $\mathcal L$ is a linear space of operators from $X$ to $Y$ satisfying $\rlinop {X} {Y} \subset \mathcal L \subset \blinop {X} {Y}$. nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 24
nodes.statement:
It is well known that implication $1 \Rightarrow 2$ is satisfied for any ordered linear space $\mathcal L$.
Implication $2 \Rightarrow 3$ follows from either Proposition~\ref {suprtrdpf} or Proposition~\ref {suprtrdp}.
Implication $3 \Rightarrow 4$ is trivial.
Observe that the cone $X_r$ is generating for $X$,
and by Proposition~\ref {isameorder} space $X$ ordered by $X_r$ generates the same order in
$\linop {X} {Y}$ as does $X$ ordered by $X_+$.
Proposition~\ref {lrdp} proves the implication $4 \Rightarrow 5$.
Suppose now that Condition~5 of Theorem~\ref {grkf} is staisfied.
Then Proposition~\ref {lrdptorkf} implies that for any $T \in \mathcal L$ we have $\rktps {T} \in \mathcal L$,
and from Proposition~\ref {rktinf} it follows that $\rktps {T} = T^+ = T \vee 0$ in $\mathcal L$,
so $\mathcal L$ is a lattice (since then for any $S, T \in \mathcal L$ expression $(T - S)^+ + S$ provides the supremum $S \vee T$ of $\{S, T\}$).
We have thus verified implication $5 \Rightarrow 1$.
Finally, if Condition~1 is satisfied
then for any $T \in \mathcal L$ we have a decomposition $T = T \vee 0 - (-T) \vee 0$ into a difference of two positive linear maps that belong to
$\mathcal L$, so $\mathcal L \subset \rlinop {X} {Y}$, and the converse inclusion was assumed.
Thus $\mathcal L = \rlinop {X} {Y}$.
Of course, Condition~1 means that $\sup T$ exists in $\mathcal L$ for a finite $T \subset \mathcal L$,
so $\sup T = \rkts {T}$ follows from either Theorem~\ref {suprtf} or Theorem~\ref {suprt}.
The proof of Theorem~\ref {grkf} is complete.
